articles.summary: The International Trade Administration (ITA) announces the launch of the U.S. Resources Management Industry Listing (RMIL), or "industry listing." The RMIL is intended to identify U.S. companies operating in water and wastewater treatment; waste management and recycling, including critical minerals recycling; air quality measuring, monitoring and control; monitoring and instrumentation; weather and forecasting; and other resources management sectors for informational, engagement, and p...
articles.full_text: The International Trade Administration (ITA) announces the launch of the U.S. Resources Management Industry Listing (RMIL), or "industry listing." The RMIL is intended to identify U.S. companies operating in water and wastewater treatment; waste management and recycling, including critical minerals recycling; air quality measuring, monitoring and control; monitoring and instrumentation; weather and forecasting; and other resources management sectors for informational, engagement, and policy support purposes. The RMIL will provide a platform for U.S. companies to market their products and services, raising their visibility with international buyers seeking to purchase U.S. resources management solutions. The RMIL supports ITA's efforts to promote American technologies and services to overseas partners and position U.S. companies to compete for international project opportunities. Eligible companies may now apply to be listed in the RMIL. The industry listing will be published online and will be maintained by the International Trade Administration's Office of Energy and Environmental Industries.

articles.title: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's exports to the United States surged 69.1 per cent to RM282.07 billion in the first nine months of this year, despite additional US tariffs on some Malaysian goods.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said total trade between Malaysia and the US rose 39.6 per cent to RM378.70 billion from January to September.
"This strong export performance was driven mainly by a surge in demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres," Johari said in a written parliamentary reply.
He was responding to Amirudin Shari (PH-Gombak), who asked about the impact of US tariffs on Malaysian industries this year and efforts to identify new markets for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
Johari said Malaysia had also benefited from an exemption from additional US tariffs on most semiconductor and E&E products.
"This decision by the US underscores the reliance of the US supply chain on the E&E sector."
The E&E sector accounts for about 64.2 per cent of Malaysia's exports to the US, with semiconductors making up 44 per cent of E&E exports.
Johari said the ministry had identified products heavily reliant on the US market that were subject to additional tariffs and did not qualify for exemptions.
The US accounts for about 32 to 47 per cent of Malaysia's exports of rubber gloves, furniture and medical devices.
Exports of rubber gloves to the US fell 1.6 per cent to RM5 billion from RM5.1 billion a year earlier.
Furniture exports declined 19.2 per cent to RM3.77 billion from RM4.67 billion, while medical device exports dropped 12 per cent to RM8.74 billion from RM9.93 billion.
He said some key industries had come under pressure to absorb additional tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to remain competitive and retain access to the US market.
Diversifying export destinations and reducing reliance on any single market remained the best way to limit exposure to external shocks, he said.
The ministry was pursuing free trade agreements and exploring non-traditional markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
It was also supporting SMEs through grants, incentives and trade and investment missions.
Malaysia's rubber glove exports recorded growth in several non-traditional markets, including Oman (712 per cent), Brazil (84.6 per cent), Sweden (80.8 per cent), Denmark (48.1 per cent), the Netherlands (43.7 per cent), Estonia (34 per cent) and Canada (18.4 per cent).
Medical device exports also increased in South Korea (206 per cent), Singapore (74.9 per cent), Sweden (65 per cent), Brazil (59.1 per cent), Türkiye (43.9 per cent), Canada (26.6 per cent) and the United Kingdom (5 per cent).
Furniture exports rose sharply in Guyana (586.1 per cent), Taiwan (140 per cent), Switzerland (135.4 per cent), Vietnam (99 per cent) and New Zealand (68.3 per cent).
Johari said the ministry would keep monitoring US trade policy and act proactively to protect exporters and reduce the tariff impact on SMEs.
The US imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on nearly all Malaysian exports on July 24 after a Section 301 investigation into forced-labour allegations.
Tariff rates from a separate US probe into industrial excess capacity have yet to be determined.

articles.title: Miti: Malaysia’s exports to US surge 69pc despite tariffs, powered by AI boom - Malay Mail
articles.summary: Miti: Malaysia’s exports to US surge 69pc despite tariffs, powered by AI boom  Malay Mail
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — Malaysia’s exports to the United States surged 69.1 per cent to RM282.07 billion for January to September 2026, while total trade between the two countries rose 39.6 per cent to RM378.70 billion.
The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) said Malaysia’s trade performance with the US continues to grow despite its exports being subjected to additional tariffs following investigations under various legal instruments conducted by the US.
According to the ministry, the strong export performance was mainly driven by a surge in demand for electrical and electronic (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following rapid developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres.
“A critical factor driving this growth is Malaysia’s strategic advantage in receiving exemptions from additional tariffs imposed by the US on most semiconductor and E&E products,” said Miti in a written response published on the Parliament’s website on Tuesday.
The ministry was responding to Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari (PH-Gombak), who sought to know the impact of US tariff impositions on Malaysia’s industry in 2026 and the new alternative markets being explored to enable micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to export their goods.
The ministry noted that the E&E sector accounts for about 64.2 per cent of Malaysia’s total exports to the US, with 44 per cent of E&E exports comprising semiconductor products.
However, Miti said that in the same period, Malaysia’s rubber glove exports to the US decreased by 1.6 per cent to RM5.0 billion, furniture exports fell by 19.2 per cent to RM3.77 billion, and medical device exports dropped by 12.0 per cent to RM8.74 billion.
He said several key Malaysian industries are under pressure to absorb US tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to maintain product competitiveness, continue exports, and preserve access to that market.
“Miti believes that efforts to diversify markets and reduce excessive dependence on any single market are the best steps to minimise exposure to external shocks and to enhance the country’s trade resilience.
“In this regard, Miti continues to actively work to enhance market access and open new markets through various free trade agreements (FTAs) that have been signed, in addition to exploring non-traditional markets in West Asia, Africa, Latin America, and South Asia,” it added.
Meanwhile, in a separate reply to Mohd Syahir Che Sulaiman (PN-Bachok), Miti said it is finalising the implementation of the New Incentive Framework (NIF) for the services sector, following its rollout for the manufacturing sector from March 1, 2026.
According to the ministry, the NIF shifts the tax incentive approach from a product- and activity-based system to a performance-based approach, with greater emphasis on outcomes and the economic impact generated by a project.
Miti said this in response to Mohd Syahir’s question about the reforms in the investment application evaluation process to ensure added value to the national economy, particularly through the creation of quality jobs. — Bernama

articles.title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry - CNBC
articles.summary: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry  CNBCWhy sales of vehicles made in the U.S. have hit a new low in Canada  Detroit Free PressAs Trump’s Tariff Threat Lingers, Autos Warn of ‘inoperable’ Effects  MichAutoColumn: Trump tariffs not working according to actual data  Automotive NewsHow US Tariffs Harm America’s Auto Industry  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a “catastrophic” scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday. 
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don’t reach a deal.
“That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry,” Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.
Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.
Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.
Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of “ripping off the United States of America for years.”
Thomas said she is “cautiously optimistic” that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.
She said she’s encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.
“Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive,” Thomas said. “It’s integral to our success.”
Honda is the second-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.
While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.
“I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this,” Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.
The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

articles.title: Trump promised 300,000 tons of beef imports at lower tariff rates to reduce grocery costs. Instead, shipments have lagged and prices haven’t budged - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Trump promised 300,000 tons of beef imports at lower tariff rates to reduce grocery costs. Instead, shipments have lagged and prices haven’t budged  Yahoo FinanceTrump’s Plan to Import More Ground Beef Is Falling Short  The New York TimesTrump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports  Al JazeeraExperts: Beef is Enjoying a Moment Culturally and Economically, but Questions Loom Large on Horizon  Arkansas Money & PoliticsHigh beef...
articles.full_text:
At the nexus of an ongoing affordability crisis and midterm election push, the Trump administration's effort to reduce beef prices appears to be falling short.
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation in August to temporarily increase the quantity of beef in the U.S. by importing 300,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings into the country at a reduced tariff rate. The imports were scheduled over 90 days, from September through November.
"This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again," Trump wrote on Truth Social announcing the policy.
But as of Oct. 19, the U.S. has imported just 59,423 metric tons of beef, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data, or just 20% of the target. And ground beef averaged $6.79 per pound as of September, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, down from $6.92 in August, but still above $6.32 a year ago.
This 7% year-over-year increase in beef prices, due to persistently high demand as well as dwindling herd sizes, has far outpaced the 2.5% to 2.9% hike in overall U.S. grocery prices, which has become representative of America's affordability woes. Trump has identified beef prices as a key issue to address during the second half of his term, as he targets policy toward the typically loyal Republican base of farmers.
"It really became unacceptable to the voter," Trump said last month. "And we do have to get elected, because if we're not going to get elected, your ranchers and your farmers are in big trouble."
But both farmers and agricultural economists are doubtful that 300,000 tons of imported beef will deliver price cuts, arguing the initiative is ineffective at best, and a financial strain during an already challenging period for the industry at worst.
"The simple assumption there was that if we can just increase supply of beef in the U.S., that should lower prices," Derrell Peel, a professor of agribusiness specializing in livestock at Oklahoma State University, told Fortune. "Unfortunately, the beef industry is much more complex than that."
The White House said Trump has done more to support American agriculture "than anyone."
"He is delivering on his promise to consumers by reducing beef prices while allowing our American beef herd to grow," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Fortune in a statement. "The President will continue taking actions to support our great farmers while driving economic prosperity for all Americans."

articles.title: Western Australia, France Sign Critical Minerals Deal - Mirage News
articles.summary: Western Australia, France Sign Critical Minerals Deal  Mirage News
articles.full_text:
- Letter of Intent deepens co-operation on critical minerals, research, skills, and investment
- Partnership will support DiversifyWA principles, creating opportunities for jobs and industry growth in Western Australia
- Agreement reinforces Western Australia's position as a trusted global supplier of critical raw materials and a partner of choice in the energy transition
Western Australia has strengthened its ties with France following the signing of a joint communique to build more resilient critical minerals supply chains, strengthen research and skills, as well as unlocking trade and investment opportunities.
The Letter of Intent (LOI) underscores Western Australia's commitment to sustainable and responsible mining practices while deepening co-operation in areas critical to the global energy transition.
Western Australia State Development Minister David Michael co-signed the LOI at the International Mining and Resources Conference + Expo in Sydney on Wednesday, 28 October 2026.
The partnership will create opportunities to strengthen collaboration across downstream and midstream processing, recycling and other value-adding activities, supporting local jobs, building industry capability, and contributing to a more resilient critical minerals supply chain.
It also highlights Western Australia's growing geopolitical and strategic importance to international partners, reinforcing our position as a trusted and reliable partner of choice.
The agreement combines Western Australia's world-leading mining expertise and growing capability in processing its significant endowment of critical raw materials, with France's expertise in mineral processing, metallurgy, engineering, and industrial technologies.
France is Australia's tenth-largest source of foreign direct investment, with two-way trade between Western Australia and France valued at more than $900 million.
The LOI provides a framework to deepen bilateral trade, investment and collaboration, supporting Western Australia's economic diversification while contributing to France's clean energy and industrial resilience ambitions.
More than 50 French companies are active in or export to Western Australia, while more than 20 Western Australian companies operate in or export to France, demonstrating the strength of the existing commercial relationship and the potential for future growth.
As stated by State Development Minister David Michael:
"This Letter of Intent demonstrates the strategic importance of Western Australia in the global critical minerals sector and the growing interest from international partners in working with our State.
"Strengthening collaboration with France will support investment, innovation, and industry development across the critical minerals value chain.
"As demand for critical minerals continues to grow, Western Australia is well placed to leverage its resources, expertise, and industrial capability to support the energy transition.
"The Cook Labor Government is focused on building a more diversified economy, creating skilled jobs, and ensuring Western Australia remains at the forefront of industries that will power the future."
As stated by Interministerial Delegate for Ores and Metals Supplies Benjamin Gallezot:
"This Letter of Intent marks an important step towards diversifying our critical minerals supply chains and strengthening our industrial capabilities.
"It also underscores Australia's role as a key partner for France.
"By pursuing a comprehensive co-operation across the entire value chain, from industry to R&D, this Letter of Intent is the foundation for a balanced partnership between France and Western Australia."

articles.title: What Should be Done with Tariff Revenue? - Alliance for American Manufacturing
articles.summary: What Should be Done with Tariff Revenue?  Alliance for American Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
A look at a handful of proposals from this Congress and the last.
The second Trump administration has raised lots of tariffs and in so doing has brought a lots of revenue into federal government coffers. There’s been regular debate about what to do with all that money. Eliminate the income tax? Refund them? Payouts to all U.S. adults? All seem unlikely to happen, for one reason or another.
There are, however, a handful of legislative proposals made in recent Congresses there that would dedicate tariff and trade remedy revenues to specific economic, adjustment or budgetary purposes rather than allowing these receipts to simply collect at the U.S. Treasury. Here are some worth examining:
The Resilient Communities Act of 2023, introduced by Sens. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) and Bill Cassidy (R-La.), redirects revenues collected through antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) enforcement into a Commerce Department fund for economic development in communities injured by import competition. That includes communities experiencing layoffs, declining sales or reduced shifts.
This proposal revisits an idea with a long history in U.S. trade policy: using AD/CVD revenues to help those harmed by unfair trade. Under the Continued Dumping and Subsidy Offset Act of 2000 (CDSOA), commonly known as the Byrd amendment, the federal government distributed collected AD/CVD duties directly to eligible domestic producers for qualifying expenditures. These could include investments in plant and equipment, R&D, worker training, technology, raw materials and working capital. That system was ultimately short-lived; in 2003, the World Trade Organization (WTO) adopted findings that CDSOA violated U.S. obligations under the WTO Antidumping and Subsidies Agreements and General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade reached i 1994. After the United States did not bring the law into compliance, the WTO authorized several trading partners to retaliate against U.S. exports. Congress subsequently repealed the Byrd amendment, with the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) explicitly describing the repeal as bringing the United States into WTO compliance.
The Baldwin-Cassidy proposal takes a different approach to the same pool of trade enforcement revenue. Rather than distributing AD/CVD collections directly to individual companies involved in trade cases, the bill changes the mechanism and beneficiaries from direct payments for affected producers to investments supporting trade-impacted communities.
The Industrial Bank for American Manufacturing Act of 2026, introduced by Reps. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) and Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.), would establish a fund in the U.S. Treasury available to the Secretary of Commerce to finance the expansion and modernization of U.S. manufacturing and strengthen U.S. industrial capacity, economic and technological security and critical supply chains. It could provide direct loans, equity investments and grants to eligible manufacturers for expanding, modernizing or otherwise improving U.S. operations in strategically important industries, as well as expanding the production and commercialization of critical and emerging technologies. Individual awards would be capped at $500 million, with Commerce required to notify the appropriate congressional committees before making an award exceeding $100 million.
The legislation would use existing Section 301 tariffs on Chinese imports as a recurring source of capitalization for the fund. Each fiscal year, the fund would receive 50% of the revenue collected from Section 301 tariffs on goods originating in China, subject to an overall cap of $15 billion per year, along with any additional funding subsequently appropriated by Congress. The sponsors explicitly describe the proposal as redirecting tariff revenue that would otherwise go to the Treasury’s General Fund toward rebuilding the domestic industrial base.
The bill also places conditions and priorities on how the money would be deployed, including tying eligible investments to industries identified through federal supply chain assessments and to critical and emerging technologies. It also establishes restrictions intended to prevent recipients from using federal support for certain activities outside the United States or in countries of concern. The bill also contains labor and workforce requirements and gives priority to certain investments, including projects in areas that have experienced significant manufacturing job losses.
The Build America Fund Act, introduced by Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), would establish a “Manufacturing Sovereign Wealth Fund” designed to rebuild U.S. industrial capacity, reduce dependence on foreign supply chains, strengthen domestic control over strategic production, support advanced manufacturing and create high-quality jobs, particularly in regions affected by deindustrialization. The legislation envisions the federal government acting as a long-term investor in strategically important manufacturing rather than relying solely on traditional grants or tax incentives. The fund could make equity investments, loans and loan guarantees, with investment returns reinvested in industrial, technological and community development.
The bill would initially capitalize the fund with $310 billion in scheduled federal appropriations, while establishing several recurring revenue streams intended to support the fund over time. Most relevant to trade policy, the bill would direct all Section 232 and Section 301 duties on automobiles, as well as all antidumping and countervailing duties, into the fund. Additional financing would come from a 1% fee on mergers and acquisitions exceeding $1 billion, a 0.1% stock-trading fee on certain high-volume sellers, a stock buyback fee, fees imposed on certain manufacturers that offshore production, and revenue from increasing the corporate tax rate from 21% to 22%. The fund would also retain interest, dividends and proceeds generated by its investments, creating a mechanism through which federal investments could generate additional capital for future industrial investments.
A notable feature is the bill’s approach to federal equity investments. When the fund takes an equity stake in a company, the legislation provides for a federal “golden share,” giving the fund special rights intended to protect the government’s strategic investment. Those rights include authority relating to major corporate decisions involving offshoring, foreign sales, transfers of intellectual property, supply chain changes and mass layoffs. In other words: The government would not necessarily need a controlling ownership stake to retain leverage over corporate decisions that could undermine its domestic industrial capacity objectives.
The Tariff Relief for American Development and Employment (TRADE) Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. John James (R-Mich.), would create a tariff-funded program intended to preserve tariffs as a U.S. trade and national security tool while providing targeted assistance to American manufacturers, farmers, workers and supply chains that experience disproportionate economic harm from tariffs or foreign retaliation. The bill explicitly seeks to use a portion of tariff revenue to strengthen U.S. productive capacity; reduce the instances of otherwise competitive companies from cutting production or jobs because of tariff-related costs; and encourage domestic investment and reshoring.
The bill would establish a tariff impact relief program administered by Commerce in consultation with Treasury and USTR. To qualify, businesses would have to demonstrate substantial U.S. production or related domestic activity and document a material net economic injury associated with tariffs. Recipients would face domestic production and employment requirements, including restrictions on using assistance to shift production overseas. Assistance could support needs such as payroll, working capital, domestic investment, sourcing, worker training and productivity improvements.
The legislation would finance this assistance through a new fund, using customs duty revenue generated by covered tariff actions, rather than relying on general revenues. As such, the structure is intended to recycle a portion of the revenue produced by tariffs back into U.S. businesses and productive capacity affected by those same trade measures.
Rep. Julia Letlow (R-La.) introduced H.R. 3982, a bill to establish a Tariff Response and Damages to Exports (TRADE) fund to provide assistance to U.S. agricultural producers affected by trade-related market disruptions. The legislation would authorize the president to deposit into the fund revenues collected from duties imposed on imports classified under chapters 1 through 24 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, which generally encompass agricultural and food products. The U.S. Secretary of Agriculture would use the fund to make payments to producers affected by export competition, reduced access to foreign markets or other trade-related disruptions, including decreased exports, foreign tariff or non-tariff barriers and increased costs of goods used in agricultural production.
The Tariff Revenue Used to Secure Tomorrow Act, or TRUST Act, introduced by Nathaniel Moran (R-Tex.), takes a substantially different approach by directing certain tariff revenues toward federal deficit reduction rather than industrial investment or trade-related assistance. If the United States maintains a budget deficit for Fiscal Year 2026 and the subsequent fiscal year, duties collected in that subsequent year above the amount collected in FY2025 would be deposited into a trust fund and then transferred to the general Treasury solely for deficit reduction.

articles.title: National Exports Grow 6% Despite Regional Tensions, Supply Chain Disruptions - The Jordan News Agency - وكالة الانباء الاردنية
articles.summary: National Exports Grow 6% Despite Regional Tensions, Supply Chain Disruptions - The Jordan News Agency  وكالة الانباء الاردنية
articles.full_text:
26/10/2026 | 10:42:28
Amman, Oct. 26 (Petra) -- The national exports increased by 6 percent during the first eight months of 2026, reaching JD6.464 billion, up from JD6.098 billion in the same period last year, as the country's industrial sector maintained growth despite regional tensions and disruptions to trade and supply chains.
The increase was supported by stronger exports of several major industrial products, including knitted apparel and related goods, which rose 4.6 percent, nitrogenous and chemical fertilizers by 16.4 percent, pharmaceutical products by 1.8 percent and crude potash by 12.3 percent.
Exports to key international markets also recorded significant gains, rising 28.9 percent to Syria, 74.3 percent to China and 11.4 percent to the European Union.
Industry leaders said the figures highlight Jordanian manufacturers' ability to maintain their presence in overseas markets, adapt to logistical challenges and expand their export destinations.
President of the Jordan and Amman Chambers of Industry Fathi Jaghbir told the Jordan News Agency (Petra) that the growth reflects the resilience of Jordan's industrial sector and the continued competitiveness of its products in international markets.
He said manufacturers had faced rising shipping and insurance costs, disruptions to transport routes and delays in the delivery of raw materials and production inputs, placing additional pressure on operating costs.
Despite these challenges, Jordanian industries maintained production and fulfilled export commitments, demonstrating their ability to respond to changing regional conditions, he added.
Jaghbir noted that export growth was not confined to a single industry but extended across several manufacturing sectors, indicating a broader and more diversified export base.
He stressed that the positive performance does not mean regional tensions have had no impact on businesses, but rather reflects the industrial sector's ability to manage disruptions while sustaining operations.
Jaghbir called for continued diversification of export markets and products to reduce dependence on individual destinations and strengthen manufacturers' resilience to external shocks.
He also emphasized the need to expand higher-value manufacturing, lower production and transportation costs, improve market access and capitalize on Jordan's international trade agreements.
The priority, he said, is to turn the current increase into sustained export growth that supports industrial investment, expands production capacity and creates employment opportunities.
He added that the performance reinforces the importance of manufacturing as a driver of economic growth and a key contributor to the objectives of Jordan's Economic Modernization Vision.
President of the Jordan Exporters Association, Senator Ahmad Khodari, said the latest figures demonstrate the strength of Jordan's industrial sector and its ability to compete internationally despite regional political and economic uncertainty.
He attributed part of this resilience to Jordan's security and stability, which have helped businesses maintain production and export operations amid regional challenges.
Khodari said the expansion into new markets is particularly significant, as it allows manufacturers to diversify their customer bases and reduce reliance on traditional export destinations.
He noted that stronger export demand can encourage manufacturers to increase production and investment, generating new jobs and supporting efforts to reduce unemployment.
Growing exports also strengthen foreign currency inflows and support the balance of payments, contributing to the country's overall economic and monetary stability, he added.
Khodari said continued export expansion aligns with the Economic Modernization Vision's priorities of improving industrial competitiveness, attracting investment and creating sustainable employment.
He highlighted the progress Jordanian manufacturers have made in modernizing production lines, adopting advanced technologies and improving product quality and standards, enabling them to enter new international markets.
Jordanian products have established a presence in Singapore and South Korea, he said, reflecting the industry's expanding international reach.
Khodari added that the Jordan Exporters Association is preparing new initiatives to strengthen access to promising markets, particularly China, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Armenia.
The association is also seeking to expand Jordan's export presence in Africa, with preparations underway to organize a trade exhibition in Kenya to introduce Jordanian products to potential buyers and establish new commercial partnerships.
He emphasized that international exhibitions remain an important platform for promoting national industries, connecting exporters with overseas importers and opening new distribution channels.
Khodari said sustaining export growth would require continued investment in manufacturing capabilities, stronger international marketing efforts and further diversification of export destinations to reinforce Jordan's position in global markets.

Notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety; request for comments; solicitation of nominations for membership.
SUMMARY:
NHTSA announces its intent to form a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety. The committee will advise the Secretary on tire safety matters through a negotiated rulemaking process. The committee will terminate when its stated objectives have been accomplished (

articles.title: Chinese Investment in the EU: Managing FSR and FDI Screening Risk - FTI Consulting
articles.summary: Chinese Investment in the EU: Managing FSR and FDI Screening Risk  FTI Consulting
articles.full_text:
- October 27, 2026
As Europe expands its scrutiny of foreign investment, outbound capital and state-linked support, Chinese companies pursuing transactions in the region increasingly need to navigate two overlapping regulatory frameworks: the European Union’s (“EU”) Foreign Subsidies Regulation (“FSR”) and the EU’s revised foreign direct investment (“FDI”) screening regime.
Under the FSR, the European Commission must be notified when an acquired company, at least one of the parties to a merger or a joint venture is established in the EU and generates at least €500 million in EU turnover, and the relevant parties to the proposed transaction have received more than €50 million in aggregate financial contributions from non-EU public authorities during the preceding three years.1
The Commission may also require prior notification for a proposed transaction that falls below the mandatory notification thresholds if it suspects that the relevant parties received foreign subsidies during the preceding three years that might distort the internal market and believes the transaction warrants ex ante review. Guidance issued in January 2026 clarified the Commission’s analytical framework for assessing distortions, applying a balancing test and exercising this case-specific notification power.2
Meanwhile, the revised FDI framework is particularly significant because it extends scrutiny beyond acquisitions of control to certain investments in sensitive sectors where governance rights or other arrangements give a non-EU investor meaningful influence over the target.3
Together, these regimes reflect a broader shift in EU transaction review: Authorities are looking not only at competition effects and ownership structures, but also at the source of financial support, the sensitivity of target assets and the level of influence an investor may obtain. FSR risk is becoming a core deal execution issue for companies pursuing EU transactions, with the potential to influence diligence scope, timetable assumptions, negotiation strategy and the conditions required to secure regulatory clearance.
What the FSR Captures — and What It Does Not
A critical distinction is that a foreign financial contribution is not the same as a foreign subsidy. Foreign financial contributions are broadly defined and can include grants, loans, loan guarantees, tax advantages and certain transactions involving goods and services. Meeting the notification thresholds only means that a transaction is subject to an FSR filing obligation; it does not mean that the foreign financial contributions concerned constitute foreign subsidies, still less that they necessarily distort the EU internal market. The Commission must first assess whether a financial contribution confers a benefit and is limited, at law or in fact, to certain one or more companies or industries. When it determines that the foreign financial contribution constitutes a foreign subsidy, the Commission must then assess whether that subsidy distorts the internal market.4
From a transaction execution perspective, however, this creates significant additional preparatory work. For example, a company considering the acquisition of EU assets must assess not only the competitive relationship between the parties, but also map relevant foreign financial contributions received across the group during the preceding three years. For a large multinational group, this may involve multiple jurisdictions, subsidiaries and financing or commercial arrangements. The information-gathering exercise itself can therefore become an important variable in the transaction timetable.
Why the FSR Matters for Chinese Companies
As a matter of law, the FSR applies to relevant financial contributions from all non-EU countries and does not target any country in particular. For Chinese companies, however, recent enforcement developments merit particular attention.
In the public procurement context, the European Commission has already launched in-depth FSR investigations involving Chinese companies. In April 2024, the Commission opened separate in-depth investigations into two bidding consortia participating in a solar photovoltaic public procurement procedure in Romania.5 One consortium included the German subsidiary of LONGi Green Energy, while the other comprised subsidiaries of Shanghai Electric.6 The Commission made clear at the time that opening an in-depth investigation did not prejudge the outcome. In May 2024, the relevant bidders withdrew from the procurement procedure, after which the Commission closed the investigations.7 These cases therefore should not be described as instances in which the Commission ultimately found that subsidies received by the Chinese companies distorted the market. They do, however, demonstrate the procedural and commercial impact that an FSR investigation can have on companies participating in EU projects.
At the same time, the Chinese government has raised explicit objections to certain aspects of EU FSR enforcement. In January 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce completed a trade and investment barrier investigation and deemed that certain practices adopted by the EU in investigations of Chinese companies under the FSR and its implementing rules constituted trade and investment barriers.8 In May 2026, China’s Ministry of Justice further determined that certain cross-border investigative measures taken against relevant Chinese entities in the EU’s FSR investigation involving Nuctech constituted unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction.9 In August 2026, the Ministry of Justice made a similar determination in relation to the EU’s FSR investigation involving JD.com.10 The Ministry of Commerce has also reiterated its hope that the EU will manage differences through dialogue and consultation and provide a fair, impartial, and predictable business environment for Chinese companies investing and operating in Europe.11
This also raises a practical issue for Chinese companies: When responding to overseas regulatory investigations, they need to also assess relevant legal obligations in China at the same time. The Provisions of the State Council on Outbound Investment, which took effect on 1 July 2026, provide that outbound investment involving technology import and export, cross-border data flows, export controls and other relevant matters must comply with applicable laws, regulations and state rules.12, 13 They also provide that where Chinese organizations or individuals involved in arbitration, litigation or investigations by overseas judicial or enforcement authorities in connection with outbound investment are compelled to provide evidence or materials overseas, those organizations or individuals must also comply with Chinese requirements concerning state secrets, data security, personal information protection, technology export controls, export controls, judicial assistance and other relevant topics.14, 15
FDI Screening: Scrutiny of Control, Influence and Sensitive Assets
The FSR is only one part of Europe’s expanding transaction review landscape. In June 2026, the EU formally adopted its revised FDI screening regulation, which will further harmonize minimum requirements for Member State screening mechanisms and require the screening of sensitive investments falling within a common minimum scope.16 The new framework will also bring certain investments made through EU subsidiaries controlled by non-EU investors within scope. Although the legislative process has been completed, the principal new rules will apply as of January 17, 2028.17
The common minimum screening scope covers dual-use and military-related items, semiconductors, quantum technologies, certain artificial intelligence technologies, strategic raw materials and critical infrastructure.18
Importantly, the trigger for FDI screening is different from traditional merger control. A minority investment that does not amount to an acquisition of control will not automatically fall outside the scope of FDI review. Under the revised regulation, an investment may fall within scope if it effectively enables an investor to participate in the management or control of the target, including through voting rights, contractual agreements, supply relationships or significant board representation.19 Purely financial investments without an intention to influence management or control are, in principle, outside this scope.
Deal structure now matters as much as deal size. When Chinese companies assess minority investments, strategic partnerships or joint ventures in Europe, they should look beyond the percentage of equity acquired. They must also consider whether governance rights, voting arrangements or board representation could influence major commercial decisions, particularly where the target controls sensitive assets, critical technologies or critical infrastructure. A minority investment that does not require notification under traditional merger control rules may nevertheless fall within the scope of FDI screening because of the influence obtained by the investor and the sensitivity of the target assets.
Why an Integrated Regulatory Strategy Matters
The practical challenge for Chinese investors is that FSR and FDI screening ask different questions but may affect the same transaction timetable. The FSR focuses on whether foreign financial contributions may constitute subsidies that distort the EU internal market, while FDI screening focuses on whether foreign ownership, influence or access may create security or public order concerns. A transaction can therefore require parallel analysis of funding history, group-level financial contributions, ownership and control, governance rights, target-sector sensitivity and the information that may need to be provided to regulators.
Taken together, the FSR and revised FDI screening framework show that EU transaction review is moving beyond traditional merger control. The final article in “Chinese Investment in the EU” wi

articles.title: How can Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in the supply chain? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: How can Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in the supply chain?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Speaking at the thematic discussion "Repositioning Vietnam - ASEAN in the Global Value Chain" within the framework of AEF 2026, Mr. Kyriakos Triantafyllidis, Director of the Center for Advanced Manufacturing and Supply Chain at the World Economic Forum (WEF), said that ASEAN has approximately 700 million people with a total economic size of about 4.3 trillion USD .
 By 2025, the region is expected to attract approximately $245 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI), a 10% increase compared to the previous year.
 According to Ms. Nguyen Thuy Lam Tuyen, General Director, Chairwoman of the Board of Directors and National CEO of ABB Vietnam, ASEAN is becoming increasingly attractive to investors thanks to three main factors: large market size, growing production capacity, and regional connectivity.
 In particular, countries like Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia , and Indonesia are investing in advanced manufacturing, digitalization, manufacturing software, and the development of skilled human resources.
 Intra-ASEAN integration remains weak, with a strong dependence on external markets.
 However, Sacha Dray, World Bank economist in Vietnam, noted that intra-ASEAN trade accounts for only about 22% of ASEAN's total merchandise exports, significantly lower than the approximately 60% of the European Union (EU).
 The cause stems from a supply-demand imbalance due to the significant income gap between the richest and poorest countries in the bloc, creating a disparity in consumer demand.
 Furthermore, despite being deeply involved in sectors such as automobiles in Thailand, assembly in Vietnam, and semiconductors in Malaysia and Singapore , the intra-regional value chain only accounts for about one-third of the level of participation in the global value chain. 
|  | 
|  Mr. Sacha Dray, World Bank economist in Vietnam, speaks at the event. Photo: Duy Hieu. | 
 According to him, the low rate of intra-regional trade makes ASEAN economies more dependent on demand from external markets such as the US and the EU. In the context of a volatile global economic environment, this dependence could make regional production and exports vulnerable to changes in international markets.
 In fact, Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Wood and Forest Products Association (VIFOREST), acknowledged that countries in the region are facing competition in major export markets such as the US, China, Japan, the EU, and South Korea .
 To enhance competitiveness, Mr. Hoai suggested that businesses need to shift from producing furniture based on popular designs to developing innovative and distinctive products. ASEAN countries should also strengthen cooperation and leverage each other's strengths instead of just competing for market share.
 Proposal to develop interconnected industrial clusters across multiple countries.
 From a state management perspective, Ms. Pham Quynh Mai, Deputy Director of the Department of Foreign Market Development ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), believes that promoting intra-bloc trade depends on reducing tariffs and improving the barriers that arise during trade.
 In addition, countries are now paying particular attention to issues such as customs procedures, electronic documents, certificates, logistics, and rules of origin. Ms. Mai emphasized that these factors impact the time and cost at each stage, from sourcing raw materials and organizing production to transportation and delivery. 
|  | 
|  Experts and policymakers have proposed various solutions to link countries in the region. Photo: Duy Hieu. | 
 Given these barriers, Ms. Mai suggested that ASEAN needs to strengthen information exchange, enhance capacity building among member states, and limit unnecessary overlapping inspection and certification requirements. Simplifying and harmonizing rules of origin could also help businesses more easily take advantage of various free trade agreements.
 Besides facilitating trade, representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade suggested that ASEAN could consider developing industrial clusters connecting large enterprises, SMEs, universities, and research centers in multiple countries in fields such as electronics, semiconductors, automobiles, and clean energy.
 According to her, countries can take on stages that suit their strengths. For example, Indonesia supplies raw materials, Malaysia participates in component manufacturing, and Thailand handles some stages of car assembly.
 This approach can help combine the strengths of each country, while promoting technology transfer, workforce training, and increasing the resilience of supply chains.

articles.title: South Korea weighs CPTPP membership as opportunity costs mount - 헤럴드경제
articles.summary: South Korea weighs CPTPP membership as opportunity costs mount  헤럴드경제
articles.full_text:
CPTPP members account for 25% of South Korea's trade; joining could generate up to 6.7 trillion won in annual manufacturing output effects
Mexico market access and cumulative rules of origin offer supply chain gains; delay risks widening competitive gap
Nearly half of South Korea's export items have lost competitiveness within the bloc since it took effect
Agriculture and fisheries face projected annual output losses of 852.3 billion won; compensation terms will determine the pace of accession
Is South Korea's membership in the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership worth the backlash from the farming and fishing industries? Joining the pact could generate up to 6.7 trillion won ($5.07 billion) in annual manufacturing output effects, but it would also reduce agricultural and fisheries production by an estimated 852.3 billion won per year. The government has slowed its push amid opposition from the farming and fishing sectors, yet analysts say CPTPP accession is not a decision South Korea can afford to keep deferring.
For an economy heavily dependent on exports, expanding into markets beyond the United States and China and securing a foothold in regional supply chains is an increasingly urgent task. South Korea's trade with CPTPP member states already accounts for 25 percent of its total goods trade. The longer accession is delayed, the greater the risk that South Korea loses ground to competitors within the bloc. The central question is how to maximize the economic benefits of membership while minimizing and compensating for the losses.
President Lee Jae Myung, speaking at a dialogue with farmers and fishers held at Cheong Wa Dae, called CPTPP membership "something that cannot be avoided, however frustrating," adding that "it is something that must be done for the country as a whole." He acknowledged that the politically comfortable choice would be to forgo membership, but said that "even if there is criticism, it must be done for the sake of the Republic of Korea as a whole, so that we can move to the next stage."
However, Lee said the chances that a final deal would be concluded within his term were "far greater" that it would not, signaling that negotiations would take considerable time. The government has decided not to submit a membership application this year, opting instead to consult fully with the farming and fishing communities before determining the direction forward.
CPTPP members account for 25% of South Korea's trade — diversifying beyond the US and China
CPTPP is a multilateral free trade agreement involving 12 countries, including Japan, Australia, Canada, Vietnam and the United Kingdom. The bloc represents about 14 percent of global GDP and applies high levels of tariff elimination along with common trade rules.
South Korea's trade with CPTPP member states is already substantial. According to a report published last month by the Korea Economic Research Institute titled "Open Plurilateral Cooperation: The Future of CPTPP and South Korea's Choice," South Korea's goods trade with the 12 CPTPP members totaled about $341 billion last year, accounting for 25 percent of its total goods trade — more than its trade with China ($273 billion, 20 percent) and the United States ($196 billion, 15 percent), its two largest trading partners.
Given how heavily South Korea depends on trade with China and the United States, diversifying its trading partners is essential to reducing exposure to shifts in the trade environment. Both countries have free trade agreements with South Korea, but tariffs, export controls and other trade issues are growing more complex, prompting calls for a broader network of cooperation beyond existing trade ties.
Consolidating South Korea's existing trade relationships with CPTPP members under a single set of rules is also cited as a benefit of joining. South Korea has bilateral or multilateral agreements with 10 of the 12 CPTPP members, but the scope and level of market opening differ across those agreements. It has no separate bilateral FTA with Japan or Mexico.
Jeffrey Schott, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said at an international seminar jointly hosted by the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and the Federation of Korean Industries on Aug. 31 that the value of CPTPP membership lies in managing existing trade relationships under common rules. He also said membership would allow South Korea to participate in shaping new trade norms covering data, labor and the environment, beyond tariff reductions alone.
South Korea also relies on CPTPP member states for a significant share of its imports. According to the Korea Economic Research Institute report, 67 percent of South Korea's mineral product imports, 42 percent of stone and glass imports, 34 percent of machinery imports and 25 percent of electronics and electrical machinery imports come from CPTPP members.
The report said the priority should be managing supply chain risks through predictable rules and dispute resolution procedures, rather than eliminating dependence on member states altogether.
CPTPP membership alone would not eliminate all risks from disruptions to key raw material supplies or economic coercion. The report noted that the current agreement lacks sufficient institutional mechanisms for coordinating industrial policy and responding jointly to supply chain crises. South Korea must therefore weigh not only the direct tariff benefits of joining but also the strategic value of participating in the formation of future trade norms.
Why join when FTAs already exist? Mexico market access and cumulative rules of origin
Mexico is the market where CPTPP membership would deliver the most direct economic benefits. Since January this year, Mexico has raised tariffs on 1,463 product categories — including automobiles and steel — by up to 50 percent for countries without a free trade agreement.
Japan can access tariff benefits through its Economic Partnership Agreement with Mexico and through CPTPP, but South Korea has no FTA with Mexico and must bear the higher tariffs. Korean automakers with local factories that source parts from South Korea may also face increased costs.
If South Korea joins CPTPP and the agreement enters into force, there would be room to reduce the tariff burden in the Mexican market. The actual benefits will depend on the outcome of accession negotiations, the date the agreement takes effect, and the tariff elimination schedules and rules of origin for individual product categories.
Another advantage is the ability to treat production processes spanning multiple member states as a single supply chain. CPTPP's cumulative rules of origin allow parts and materials produced in member countries to be counted together as originating within the bloc when determining origin status.
For example, if a South Korean company uses Japanese parts and Vietnamese materials to manufacture a product domestically and then exports it to Canada, those parts and materials could qualify as CPTPP-originating — provided the product meets the applicable origin criteria for its category.
Under existing bilateral FTAs, different rules of origin apply for each agreement. Under CPTPP, production processes spanning multiple member states can be managed under a common set of rules. This could benefit manufacturers that source components from multiple countries and operate production processes across several nations.
According to preliminary results of an economic impact analysis released by the government in September, South Korea's real GDP would be 0.38 percentage points higher 10 years after the agreement enters into force than it would be without membership.
The Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade estimated that production ripple effects across manufacturing and related upstream and downstream industries would increase by an annual average of 6.3 trillion to 6.7 trillion won over the 15 years following the agreement's entry into force. Production ripple effects for small and medium-sized enterprise-based industries were projected at an annual average of 1.1 trillion to 1.2 trillion won.
The figure of up to 6.7 trillion won does not represent export revenue growth or corporate net profit. It includes not only finished goods but also production induced across related industries such as parts and materials. Actual corporate gains will vary depending on tariff rates by product category, rules of origin and supply chain structure.
Competitiveness index falls for 47.7% of export items — the opportunity cost of delayed accession
Beyond the gains from joining CPTPP, South Korea also needs to weigh the opportunity cost of staying out.
A report released by the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade on Oct. 14, titled "Analysis of South Korea's Competitiveness Before and After CPTPP's Entry into Force," compared competitiveness indicators for 5,185 South Korean export items in the pre-agreement period of 2012–2018 and the post-agreement period of 2021–2024. The index fell for 2,474 items, or 47.7 percent of the total.
The analysis used the Revealed Symmetric Comparative Advantage index, which measures the relative export competitiveness of specific product categories. A decline in the index means relative competitiveness in that market has weakened.
Notably, 796 of the items that saw a decline within the CPTPP region maintained or improved their competitiveness in markets outside the bloc — meaning the same South Korean products showed divergent competitiveness trends inside and outside the region.
Across 15 manufacturing sectors — including shipbuilding, displays and automobiles — every sector where South Korea's index fell also saw CPTPP member states' index rise.

articles.title: SKF India (Industrial) Appoints Nilesh Vaidya As Head Of Seals For ISEA Region - Sahyadri Startups
articles.summary: SKF India (Industrial) Appoints Nilesh Vaidya As Head Of Seals For ISEA Region  Sahyadri Startups
articles.full_text:
Pune: SKF India (Industrial) (NSE: SKFINDUS | BSE: 544572), a technology and solutions provider for industrial applications, has appointed Nilesh Vaidya as Head of Seals for the ISEA Region, covering India and Southeast Asia.
The appointment of Nilesh Vaidya comes as demand for high-performance sealing solutions accelerates across key industrial sectors in the ISEA region.
In his new role, Nilesh will drive growth for SKF India (Industrial)’s advanced seals portfolio, with a focus on market share expansion, channel development, key account deepening, and building high-performing teams across diverse markets.
As Head of Seals for the ISEA Region, Nilesh Vaidya will focus on strengthening SKF’s position in the seals market across India and Southeast Asia while expanding sales channels and deepening customer relationships.
Commenting on his appointment, Nilesh Vaidya, Head of Seals, ISEA, SKF India (Industrial), said, “As I take on this role, my priority is clear: strengthen SKF’s position in the seals market across India and Southeast Asia.
Growth will come from getting closer to customers, deepening key account partnerships and strengthening the channels that connect our expertise to local needs.
Together with our teams and partners, I will focus on translating SKF’s sealing capabilities into measurable customer value and that value into sustained business growth.”
Nilesh Vaidya brings nearly 25 years of leadership experience spanning industrial manufacturing, process automation, and water technologies. He has a track record of business expansion across India and Southeast Asia.
His regional market knowledge, channel expertise, and multi-country leadership experience are expected to support the growth of SKF India (Industrial)’s seals business.
Prior to joining SKF India (Industrial), Nilesh Vaidya served as Managing Director at GF Piping Systems in Jakarta, where he led the business across mining, industrial utilities, and building technologies.
Before that, Nilesh Vaidya spent nearly seven years at Danaher Corporation. During his tenure, he led growth strategy for the Water Quality Platform as Director, Business Development for South ASEAN and also held leadership roles at Hach India.
Earlier in his career, Nilesh Vaidya spent more than a decade at Sandvik Coromant. He began his professional career at Kirloskar Oil Engines.
With experience across industrial manufacturing, process automation and water technologies, Nilesh Vaidya will lead SKF India (Industrial)’s seals business across India and Southeast Asia, with a focus on market share expansion, channel development, key accounts and team building.

articles.title: 2026 International Exchange Conference on Industrial Vertical Foundation Models, Industrial Design, and Intelligent Manufacturing of Precision Molds Held in Shenzhen - FinancialContent
articles.summary: 2026 International Exchange Conference on Industrial Vertical Foundation Models, Industrial Design, and Intelligent Manufacturing of Precision Molds Held in Shenzhen  FinancialContent
articles.full_text:
SHENZHEN, China - October 26, 2026 - The 2026 International Exchange Conference on Industrial Vertical Foundation Models, Industrial Design, and Intelligent Manufacturing of Precision Molds was successfully held in Shenzhen on October 20.
Under the theme “Innovating Industrial Design with Industrial Vertical Foundation Models; Consolidating the Foundation of a Manufacturing Powerhouse through Intelligent Manufacturing of Precision Molds”, the conference brought together government representatives, academicians, industry experts, university scholars, diplomatic representatives from Belt and Road partner countries, leading domestic and international enterprises, investment institutions, and industry associations.
The event established an international dialogue platform connecting government bodies, industry, academia, research institutions, technology end-users, and financial capital. Discussions focused on AI-powered mold design, mold flow simulation, localization of industrial software, and cross-border industrial collaboration.
Participants explored new approaches to integrating artificial intelligence into precision manufacturing and advancing the development of China's manufacturing sector.
Emerging Opportunities: AI and Manufacturing Converge as Shenzhen Strengthens Its Industrial Innovation Ecosystem
The rapid convergence of artificial intelligence and manufacturing technologies is transforming industrial design. Industrial Vertical Foundation Models are increasingly being developed to address specialized manufacturing challenges and improve production efficiency.
The mold industry, often described as the "mother of manufacturing," plays a foundational role in advanced industrial production and is closely linked to the competitiveness of the manufacturing sector.
Traditional mold manufacturing has long faced challenges such as lengthy R&D cycles, heavy reliance on imported simulation software, barriers to transferring manufacturing know-how, and shortages of highly skilled professionals. These challenges have created growing demand for technological innovation and industrial transformation.
Shenzhen is home to internationally competitive mold manufacturing and consumer electronics industry clusters, supported by comprehensive supply chains and an integrated industrial ecosystem covering research and development, design, prototyping, and mass production.
These advantages make the city an important testbed for real-world deployment of industrial AI technologies.
The conference was held with guidance and support from the Organizing Committee of the World United Design Conference and the Global Think Tank of the China International Creative Design Promotion Week.
It was jointly organized by the Global Chinese United General Chamber of Commerce, the Shenzhen Enterprise Confederation, the Shenzhen Entrepreneurs Association, and the Shenzhen Enterprise Management Association.
Shenzhen ModelAI Technology Research Co., Ltd. (ModelAI) served as a Special Invited Host., with additional support from several participating institutions.
The event brought together resources from technology, manufacturing, investment, and international cooperation to promote collaboration across the industrial value chain.
Attendees included former senior officials from China's Ministry of Science and Technology, Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission, and Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, alongside academicians, university researchers, representatives of industry associations, as well as executives from leading enterprises and investment institutions.
Diplomatic and trade representatives from the Central African Republic, Madagascar, Pakistan, Ethiopia, France, Saudi Arabia, and other countries also attended.
Their participation highlighted the conference's international scope and created opportunities for China's precision manufacturing sector to strengthen connections with overseas markets.
Expert Perspectives: Defining Practical Pathways for Industrial AI in Intelligent Manufacturing
During the conference, distinguished speakers shared perspectives on industrial development, enterprise applications, national policies, design philosophy, and technological innovation.
Participants stressed that achieving greater technological self-reliance in manufacturing requires more than adopting general-purpose large AI models. Instead, development built on Industrial Vertical Foundation Models must focus on specialized applications and translate large-model capabilities into tangible productivity gains in mold design, simulation analysis, and manufacturing-process optimization.
Professor Liu Guanzhong of Tsinghua University, widely recognized as a pioneering figure in Chinese industrial design, delivered a presentation titled "The Way of Great Design: The Direction of Chinese Industrial Design and Manufacturing in the AI Era."
He emphasized that industrial design in the age of artificial intelligence should extend beyond aesthetic improvements and return to the fundamental needs of manufacturing, while redefining the value system of Chinese industrial design.
Wu Zhongze, former Vice Minister of Science and Technology of China, discussed how artificial intelligence could empower the real economy and outlined practical approaches to deploying Industrial Vertical Foundation Models in manufacturing environments.
Tan Jianrong, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, examined technological directions for intelligent transformation in the precision mold industry, providing academic insights into future industrial innovation.
Tan Lingyun, founder of Shenzhen ModelAI Technology Research Co., Ltd., shared the company's experience in developing and deploying Industrial Vertical Foundation Models in intelligent mold manufacturing.
Drawing on practical experience in technology entrepreneurship, Tan discussed the industry's challenges and explored ways to bridge the gap between AI innovation and factory-level implementation.
From a broader policy perspective, Zhang Jing'an, an academician of the International Eurasian Academy of Sciences, and Jiang Yaoping, former Vice Minister of Commerce of China, highlighted the importance of localizing industrial software, encouraging collaborative innovation among industry, universities, and research institutions, and improving the industrial ecosystem for specialized AI companies.
A French business representative also shared perspectives on international industrial cooperation and expressed expectations for deeper collaboration between Chinese and overseas manufacturing enterprises through emerging AI technologies.
The keynote presentations addressed macroeconomic strategy, industrial policy, academic research, and practical manufacturing applications, helping establish a shared understanding of the opportunities and challenges facing industrial AI.
Launch Ceremonies: Advancing Chinese Industrial AI Technologies into International Markets
Following the keynote discussions, the conference held two major launch ceremonies marking the beginning of a series of industrial development initiatives.
The first ceremony officially launched the conference.
More than ten distinguished guests, including Tan Lingyun, Fang Zhenlong, Wu Zhongze, Jiang Yaoping, Zhang Qin, Zhang Jing'an, Tan Jianrong, Liu Guanzhong, Chen Dongliang, and Xu Shouzhen, appeared on stage to inaugurate the event.
The ceremony marked the formal opening of an international gathering dedicated to Industrial Vertical Foundation Models and intelligent manufacturing of precision molds.
The second ceremony launched the ModelAI Belt and Road Market Expansion Initiative.
Tan Lingyun and Qin Taiming joined diplomatic representatives and international business delegates on stage to announce the initiative, which aims to expand overseas markets for Chinese industrial AI technologies.
Industrial cooperation is a central component of the Belt and Road Initiative. China's precision manufacturing technologies and innovations in industrial AI are increasingly seeking opportunities to serve international markets.
The launch established a new channel connecting Chinese industrial AI enterprises with overseas diplomatic and commercial networks.
The initiative aims to support the international deployment of independently developed Industrial Vertical Foundation Models through technology exports, project cooperation, and partnerships with overseas manufacturers.
It also seeks to strengthen the participation of Chinese intelligent manufacturing enterprises in global industrial value chains.
Together, the two ceremonies represented important milestones for the conference.
The first focused on integrating domestic industrial resources and strengthening the innovation ecosystem, while the second emphasized international market development and cross-border cooperation.
Cooperation Agreements: Bridging Industry, Academia, and Investment Partners to Advance Real-World Projects
The conference translated discussions into concrete actions through five groups of cooperation agreements and two recognition ceremonies.
The agreements covered industry-academia-research collaboration, commercialization of scientific and technological achievements, intellectual property protection, strategic industrial partnerships, and investment cooperation.
In the field of industry-academia collaboration, Shenzhen ModelAI Technology Research Co., Ltd. signed an agreement with Associate Professor Xiang Yi of South China University of Technology to establish a joint laboratory for an intelligent industrial software research and innovation platform.
The partnership aims to connect university research resources with industrial applications and support innovation in domestically developed industrial software.
