articles.title: Vietnam cashew sector looks to reshape global supply chains - Thông tấn xã Việt Nam
articles.summary: Vietnam cashew sector looks to reshape global supply chains  Thông tấn xã Việt Nam
articles.full_text:
Illustrative image.  Photo: VNA  
The event, themed “From raw materials to added value - Connecting value chains and shaping the future of global cashew supply chains,” was organised by the Vietnam Cashew Association (VINACAS) in coordination with the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
According to VINACAS Chairman Pham Van Cong, Vietnam exported nearly 800,000 tonnes of cashew nuts in 2025, earning a record 5.4 billion USD. For nearly two decades, the country has led the world in cashew processing and exports, accounting for more than 80% of global exports.
However, shifting tariff policies, trade barriers, and rising production, transport, logistics, and financial costs are putting pressure on the entire value chain. The industry must address immediate challenges while pursuing a long-term strategy for the next 10–20 years, with a focus on deeper processing, product diversification and higher-value products rather than semi-processed exports.
Cong stressed that cashew production is part of a global supply and value chain in which stakeholders’ interests are closely linked. Sustainable development therefore depends on cooperation among countries, suppliers, processors and distributors, rather than individual efforts. Stakeholders should improve market transparency, share data on supply, demand and price fluctuations, and jointly manage opportunities and risks.|
Tran Ngoc Hai, a representative from the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency, said the cashew industry faces long-term structural challenges. He noted that shifting global supply chains, sustainability-related technical barriers, rising demand for green consumption and competition from raw-material-producing countries are forcing businesses to rethink their export strategies.
Vietnam imports around 80% of the raw cashew nuts used for processing, while land available for domestic cultivation is increasingly limited. This dependence underscores the need to secure supplies, improve processing efficiency and increase the value of finished products.
Hai urged businesses to shift from selling existing products to offering higher-value goods, while building brands and establishing a direct presence in overseas markets. He said the ministry plans to modernise trade promotion, using artificial intelligence (AI) and big data for market forecasting, promoting green and digital trade, and helping businesses meet international standards.
These efforts are linked to the 2026–2030 programme for expanding into international markets, approved by the Prime Minister, which aims to help businesses improve management, build brands, identify target markets, develop distribution channels and integrate more deeply into global value chains.
Cashew companies should fully tap available support mechanisms to develop and protect their brands, expand deep processing and introduce Vietnamese-branded products into international distribution networks, reducing reliance on foreign partners’ labels, Hai said.
Ashok Krishen, Chairman of the International Nut and Dried Fruit Council (INC), said the global nut market had grown by an average of around 8% annually over the past decade. Annual demand for nuts and dried fruit stands at about 1.4 million tonnes, with cashews accounting for the largest share.
According to Krishen, consumers, particularly young people, are becoming increasingly health-conscious and paying greater attention to their diets. Vietnam’s cashew sector could benefit by developing products that meet modern consumer preferences, provided businesses understand market demand, maintain quality and meet import-market requirements.
He also underlined the need to boost international cooperation to establish common quality and technical standards for nuts and dried fruit, saying harmonisation would facilitate trade and strengthen competitiveness.
Vietnam’s leading position in cashew kernel processing and exports provides a strong foundation for further integration into global value chains, he added./.

articles.title: PROCOMER supports ten Costa Rican companies seeking to expand their presence in the global aerospace supply chain - AOL.com
articles.summary: PROCOMER supports ten Costa Rican companies seeking to expand their presence in the global aerospace supply chain  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
- Companies participated in NBAA-BACE, an event that brought together more than 23,000 industry professionals and over 1,000 exhibitors.
SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica, Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ten Costa Rican companies from the aerospace sector participated in an international trade event to identify new buyers and business partners, explore opportunities to join global supply chains, and follow up on existing business opportunities with key players in the international aerospace industry. Their participation was part of a broader strategy to expand the presence of Costa Rican suppliers in this sector. Another objective was to position Costa Rica as an attractive destination for new foreign direct investment (FDI) projects in the aerospace industry.
The companies participated in the NBAA Business Aviation Convention & Exhibition (NBAA-BACE), held from October 20 to 22 in Las Vegas, United States. Recognized as one of the leading international events for business aviation, the convention brought together more than 23,000 attendees and 1,000 exhibitors from 98 countries. This marked Costa Rica's sixth participation with an exhibition space at the event.
"The aerospace industry offers opportunities for Costa Rican companies to bring their capabilities in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and technology into highly specialized international supply chains. Our participation in NBAA also showcases an increasingly diverse range of capabilities, including software, automation, maintenance, and logistics. Our goal is to continue creating opportunities for more Costa Rican suppliers to enter this industry and move toward more sophisticated, higher value-added activities, while identifying investment opportunities that contribute to strengthening and developing the country's aerospace ecosystem," stated Laura López, CEO of the Trade and Investment Promotion Agency of Costa Rica (PROCOMER).
The delegation, led by PROCOMER and the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster (CRAC), included ten companies offering capabilities across different segments of the aerospace value chain: Avionyx and Novacomp, specializing in software and hardware; Soltek and Olympic Precision Machining, in precision machining; AASA, in automation; All Jets and Global Technik, in maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO); Aerologística and Interconexiones Multimodales de Carga (IMDC), in ground handling services; and GJ Cargo and IMDC, in logistics.
Companies Target Different Segments of the Aerospace Supply Chain
During NBAA-BACE, Costa Rican companies had access to businesses involved in manufacturing, maintenance, parts and accessories, design, engineering, software, and other specialized areas. Their participation provided an opportunity to follow up on potential business deals initiated during previous editions and establish new commercial contacts.
Advertisement
The event brought together operators, manufacturers, suppliers, and other industry stakeholders involved in purchasing decisions and the evaluation of solutions and technologies for the aerospace sector. The exhibition featured everything from commercial aircraft and private jets to eVTOL (electric vertical take-off and landing) aircraft, which are powered by electricity and capable of taking off and landing vertically.
"The Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster's participation in NBAA 2026 reflects the evolution and diversification of the capabilities our country offers to the global aerospace industry. In addition to its recognized expertise in advanced precision manufacturing and specialized engineering, Costa Rica continues to strengthen an increasingly comprehensive range of aviation-related services, including maintenance, repair, technical support, engineering solutions, corporate services, and capabilities that support aircraft operations," noted Esteban Carrillo, Executive Director of the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster (CRAC).
Carrillo added that "with PROCOMER's support, this participation helps foster strategic connections between Costa Rican companies and key industry players across international markets, creating new opportunities for business, investment, and collaboration."
Participation in NBAA was part of the international promotion and foreign direct investment attraction strategy developed by PROCOMER in collaboration with the Costa Rica Aerospace Cluster. The strategy aims to strengthen the presence of Costa Rican suppliers in specialized markets and promote the country as a nearshoring destination for companies seeking manufacturing solutions and services to support their supply chains and aviation operations.
Throughout 2026, this strategy also brought companies from the sector to specialized international events, including the Aerospace Innovation Forum in Canada, Aerospace Meetings Querétaro in Mexico, and the Farnborough International Airshow in the United Kingdom.

articles.title: Morocco overtakes SA among Africa’s top five investment destinations - Business Day
articles.summary: Morocco overtakes SA among Africa’s top five investment destinations  Business Day
articles.full_text:
Morocco’s aggressive drive to build its industrial base around its automotive industry has seen it overtake South Africa in the rankings of Africa’s most attractive investment destinations, piling pressure on Pretoria to up its game in a sector that accounts for about 5% of the economy.
The latest RMB Where to Invest in Africa, published on Tuesday, puts Morocco in fourth place, pushing South Africa into fifth. Seychelles retains the top spot, followed by Mauritius and Egypt.
The study identifies Morocco’s industrial transformation as a key driver of its improved ranking, with vehicle production having doubled since 2015.
“Morocco’s figures point to sustained industrial momentum and rising external confidence, while South Africa’s point to a mature industrial base contending with weaker demand, trade headwinds and capital reversal,” the report reads.
“Morocco surpasses South Africa to emerge as the highest-ranked industrial economy in Africa over the coverage period, reflecting sustained industrial upgrading, export diversification and effective implementation of strategic industrial policies.
“While South Africa remains a continental industrial powerhouse, it continues to experience a steady decline in industrial competitiveness … Morocco’s growth story over the past year has been defined by acceleration; South Africa’s by slow recovery from prior structural constraints.”
To improve the car manufacturing industry, minister of trade, industry & competition Parks Tau said this month that the country will phase out semi-knocked-down vehicle assembly, warning that if Africa’s most industrialised economy does not build the vehicles that markets such as Europe will buy, the country will lose those markets.
The EU is the largest export destination for South Africa’s automotive industry, absorbing roughly two-thirds of all vehicles built in the country. However, the EU is facing an accelerated consumer shift to new hybrid technologies.
South Africa’s automotive master plan has set a target of increasing the percentage of locally manufactured component content from current levels (around 38%–42%) to 60%.
Paul Cooke, from Investec’s corporate and investment banking franchise, said the new-energy vehicle (NEV) transition for South Africa is now an industrial imperative.
“As demand shifts towards cleaner vehicle technologies, South Africa needs to secure a share of their production. With Europe and the UK enforcing stricter carbon measures and zero-emission requirements, failure to gear local production towards NEVs risks eroding established export markets while increasing reliance on imported vehicles,” Cooke said in a note.
“A pragmatic path will likely require flexible manufacturing across internal combustion engine, hybrid, plug-in hybrid and electric vehicle technologies while the market evolves.”
A recent report by global accounting and advisory firm PKF found that while South Africa retains important competitive strengths, including established investment by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and an extensive component-supplier network, the country will require co-ordinated action among government, manufacturers, infrastructure providers and the wider automotive ecosystem to retain these attributes.
The firm said priority areas for South Africa include accelerating localisation, improving the reliability and cost competitiveness of electricity and freight logistics, securing future vehicle production mandates, developing NEV manufacturing capabilities, and strengthening the domestic supplier base.
Ziyaad Moosa, a partner at PKF Johannesburg, said South Africa faces growing competition from automotive manufacturing hubs such as Morocco, Thailand and Mexico, which are aggressively vying for international production mandates.
“The decisions made over the next few years will determine whether the country attracts the next generation of automotive investment or gradually loses production volumes, export opportunities and industrial capacity to competing markets,” says Moosa.
“South Africa’s automotive industry remains one of the country’s strongest examples of globally integrated manufacturing. It has the potential to play an even greater role in exports, investment and employment.
“But this opportunity comes with a narrowing window of opportunity. The industry needs more than ambitious targets. It needs a competitive operating environment, faster policy execution, and the confidence of global manufacturers to commit their next generation of investment to South Africa.”
Isaah Mhlanga, chief economist at RMB, told Business Day that Morocco’s move above South Africa is best understood as a growth momentum story. Industrialisation, export diversification, infrastructure investment and macroeconomic stability have strengthened Morocco’s position.
“It’s not that South Africa has been contracting, no. It has been growing positively, but at a slower pace compared to a fast-growing Morocco, hence the overtaking of South Africa,” he said.
“Part of the story there is economic growth. Morocco has been growing at close to 5% for the last couple of years. South Africa has been stuck at 1% for the last decade. This year we’re still expecting 1%, and next year we’re expecting 1%.”
The investment bank said South Africa remains a significant investment market, supported by deep financial markets, improving reform delivery and substantial shock-absorbing capacity, but slower growth continues to place pressure on its ranking.
“There are some visible aspects, from a sector perspective, where you can actually see this happening in real time,” said Mhlanga. “Take the automotive sector. Morocco has been industrialising. Its proximity to Europe has meant that it can attract a lot of the automotive sectors that produce at low cost for exporting into the European market.”
He said the likes of Nissan had left South Africa to go to Morocco “precisely because they’ve been doing the right reforms to encourage investments into the automotive sector. We have been seeing the large established automotive manufacturers in the domestic market suffering and reducing prices when competing with the Chinese brands that are cheaper.”
Mhlanga also noted that the energy issues that South Africa had experienced in recent years due to load-shedding contributed to increasing the cost of doing business in the local market.
Another key sector in which Morocco is outperforming South Africa is tourism, with the RMB report noting that Morocco recorded 19.8-million arrivals in 2025 and receipts of about $13bn.
The African country is set for further tourism boosts as it co-hosts the 2030 Fifa World Cup with Spain and Portugal, with the country targeting 26-million annual tourists by the end of the decade.
“South Africa’s tourism recovery, while positive — a record 10.5-million international tourist arrivals in 2025, up 17.7% on 2024 — lacks a demand catalyst of comparable scale.”
South Africa has set a target of welcoming 15-million international visitors by 2030. Morocco and South Africa were on par a decade ago, both welcoming about 10-million visitors a year, while Tunisia was a distant third with 5.7-million.
The Operation Vulindlela progress report, which covers the period from April to August, notes that the country has made significant progress in areas such as visa reform. The report states that half of the reforms in this area have been met, and the rest are on track to meet their objectives.
Some of the achievements include the introduction of the trusted tour operator scheme, the trusted employer scheme, electronic travel authorisation and the meetings, exhibitions, events and tourism scheme.

articles.title: Mexico's Foreign Investment Screening Reform: A National Security Mechanism Born from Trade Politics - JD Supra
articles.summary: Mexico's Foreign Investment Screening Reform: A National Security Mechanism Born from Trade Politics  JD Supra
articles.full_text:
For most of the post-Cold War period, foreign direct investment was largely viewed as an economic benefit. Governments competed to attract foreign capital, reduce barriers to entry, and integrate into global value chains. Security-related restrictions on foreign investment generally remained limited to defense industries, weapons manufacturing, and other constitutionally protected activities, such as energy and telecommunications.1
Mexico's current investment legal framework is based on investment promotion and introduces a “negative list” approach, prohibiting or restricting foreign investment participation in certain activities. However, it does not include a screening mechanism for national security purposes. This is about to change: Mexico is on the verge of discussing a bill that amends its foreign investment regime.
Mexico’s legal overhaul should not come as a surprise. Geopolitical competition between the USA and China is the main driver behind this reform. The emergence of China as a major technological and economic power prompted many governments to reconsider whether foreign acquisitions could enable competitors to obtain strategic technologies, intellectual property, or critical infrastructure assets. The U.S. concern extends to foreign investment in allied countries, including Mexico. Since the Biden administration, U.S. officials have repeatedly encouraged Mexico to strengthen its capacity to review foreign investments on national-security grounds.2 In December 2023, U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Mexico’s Secretary of Finance announced the creation of a bilateral working group on foreign investment review. More recently, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer emphasized the importance of strengthening North American economic security and supply-chain resilience. Washington increasingly views investment screening as a regional issue, and Mexico must take steps to address it if the USMCA is to be extended.
The USMCA extension is the carrot; the threat of non-renewal, the stick. Against this backdrop, one must read the draft bill on Mexico’s foreign investment screening. The proposed reform raises several questions: does Mexico model its screening mechanism on the U.S. approach? Is there a “national security” risk-assessment test defined in the statute? What foreign investments will trigger the mechanism, and who will review the applications? This article seeks to answer these questions.
- Foreign Investment Screening in the USA: CFIUS review.
The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) is an interagency committee chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury. Originally established in 1975, CFIUS assumed its modern form through the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act (FIRRMA) of 2018, which significantly expanded its jurisdiction to cover certain non-controlling investments involving critical technologies, critical infrastructure, or sensitive personal data. As a result, minority investments may now trigger review where foreign investors obtain governance rights, board representation, or access to sensitive technologies.
The filing regime includes both voluntary and mandatory submissions of written notices and declarations. Written notices are comprehensive filings containing detailed information about the transaction and the parties involved. In contrast, declarations are abbreviated filings that provide CFIUS with basic information to assess whether further review, a written notice, or another action permitted under the Act is needed.
Mandatory filing requirements apply under two primary circumstances. First, they apply to certain covered transactions involving foreign government interests, where a foreign government has a substantial interest in a foreign person and that foreign person acquires a substantial interest in a U.S. business involving critical technology, critical infrastructure, or sensitive personal data. Second, mandatory filing requirements apply to certain covered transactions involving critical technologies, where a foreign person makes a covered investment in a U.S. business that produces, designs, tests, manufactures, fabricates, or develops critical technologies, and a U.S. regulatory authorization, such as an export license, would be required to export, reexport, or transfer that technology to a direct or indirect party to the transaction.3 In either circumstance, parties may file a full written notice instead of a declaration.4
CFIUS conducts its national-security review through a risk-based process centered on three interrelated elements. The threat analysis examines the foreign investor’s ownership structure, government links, compliance history, and capability to act contrary to U.S. interests.5 The vulnerability analysis assesses whether the target business possesses assets, technologies, or data that could be exploited to harm national security, with particular attention to critical technologies, defense-related production, telecommunications, energy systems, and strategically important supply chains. The consequence analysis evaluates the potential impact of such exploitation on military readiness, cybersecurity, technological leadership, critical infrastructure resilience, and supply-chain security.
CFIUS does not operate solely through approval or rejection. Rather than requiring the abandonment of a transaction, mitigation agreements allow CFIUS to clear transactions while addressing specific national-security risks. CFIUS mitigation measures include restrictions on access to technology or sensitive information, requirements to segregate computer networks, data or information transfer restrictions, personnel restrictions, the establishment of corporate security committees, and requirements that certain facilities, equipment, or operations remain in the United States.6 Parties must disclose ownership structures, ultimate beneficial owners, sources of financing, and governance arrangements, often extending well beyond ordinary corporate disclosure requirements.7
The Nippon Steel–U.
S.
Steel transaction illustrates these dynamics.
Although the investor originated from Japan, a close U.
S.
ally, the transaction raised national-security concerns because the steel industry is considered a strategic sector critical to supply chains; the U.
S.
had already imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 after a “national security” investigation.
The debate focused less on the investor’s nationality and more on economic resilience, domestic production capacity, and the long-term availability of steel for defense-related purposes.
After CFIUS review, President Biden initially blocked the acquisition in January 2025.
Nippon Steel and U.
S.
Steel then sued President Joe Biden, alleging he violated the companies' right to a fair review by barring CFIUS staff from negotiating a mitigation agreement and manipulating the review process toward a predetermined decision to block the transaction and "curry favor with the USW [United Steelworkers] leadership in Pennsylvania in his bid for reelection.
”8 The deal was subsequently restructured under President Trump: Nippon Steel would acquire up to 49% of U.
S.
Steel, with U.
S.
Steel remaining under American control.
The restructured deal included mitigation measures such as maintaining U.
S.
Steel’s headquarters in Pittsburgh, minimum capital investment commitments, and production guarantees.
The case demonstrates that investment reviews often operate at the intersection of security, economics, and politics.

- Mexico's Proposed Reform of the Foreign Investment Law
Currently, a foreign investment screening mechanism does exist in Mexico, but it is not a national security review. This mechanism is triggered only when the assets involved exceed an extremely high value threshold that few foreign investments have triggered in Mexico, for instance the ABINV acquisition of Grupo Modelo. Foreign Investors are required to disclose the acquisition and obtain the approval of the National Foreign Investment Commission (CNIE), but it does not entail a thorough national security review. Needless to say, Mexico’s Foreign Investment Law does provide that the CNIE has the authority to interfere in an acquisition on behalf of a foreign investment when it poses a risk to national security.9 In other words, CNIE’s powers are ex-post.
Hence, Mexico's proposed reform seeks to build-upon this national-security authority and introduces a new chapter called “National Security in Foreign Investments.” Rather than relying on a broad and largely undefined ex-post national-security power, the reform establishes an ex-ante structured review mechanism applicable to certain foreign acquisitions in strategically sensitive sectors. The CNIE will be responsible of its implementation. The initiative, therefore, represents a significant substantive and institutional development in Mexico's approach to foreign investment review.
Notably, the initiative's Exposición de Motivos (Statement of Purpose) explicitly states that the reform was developed in consideration of the principles established by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) for investment screening mechanisms: non-discrimination, transparency, predictability, proportionality, and accountability. This acknowledgment is significant because these principles closely mirror the substantive protections commonly found in Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs), such as non-discrimination (national treatment and most-favored-nation treatment), transparency, proportionality, and due process. The express reference to OECD standards suggests that Mexico is aware of the international obligations against which its screening mechanism will be measured. As currently drafted, the mechanism appears de jure consistent, however, its applications remains an open question, particularly in light of the broad definition of covere

articles.title: Practical implementation is cross-border digital ID’s weak spot - Biometric Update
articles.summary: Practical implementation is cross-border digital ID’s weak spot  Biometric Update
articles.full_text:
A workshop hosted by the Cambridge DPI Regulatory Programme and the Alan Turing Institute examined the practical barriers preventing national digital identity systems from working together across borders.
The DPI Regulatory Programme will publish reports on regulatory architecture and Singapore’s Singpass next month, followed by two reports on e-KYC, says Pavle Avramović, Cambridge Centre director of research and policy at Financial Innovation for Impact (Fii). The reports draw on an ongoing series of workshops held in different countries.
The Programme’s researchers have found that a growing number of regulators are involved with digital ID, including data protection and competition authorities, though central banks still tend to have the strongest voice.
To help understand the differences from country to country, the Fii and Cambridge Center for Alternative Finance have developed the Regulatory Diagnostic Framework (RDF), an analytical tool to help with governance reviews.
Avramović identifies infrastructure constraints, fragmented data formats across government agencies and insufficient political commitment to building trust and adoption as common interoperability challenges.
Meanwhile countries are cautiously exploring how AI can help them deliver services, which adds another wrinkle for regulators.
Governance means regulation in practice
Different digital ID architectures come with different risks and responsibilities. What they have in common is that tailored governance is important, along with guardrails for private sector participation and cross-regulatory coordination.
Avramović presented country-level findings from Uganda, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia and Kenya, which will also appear in the upcoming report.
Governance can differ significantly between theory and practice, with limited institutional capacity and human resources causing real-world breakdowns. One example Avramović mentions is when service delivery changes to prioritize new digital credentials in a way that makes an optional ID practically mandatory. Civil society organizations in Ethiopia participating in the workshops observed this problem, he says.
The situation creates a “hot potato” of responsibility, Avramović says.
Adding complexity, digital ID risks can occur anywhere in the system, depending on the context and architecture of the system. Regulators must also handle additional pressures caused by emerging technologies. Cross-regulatory sandboxes can help, but Avramović expects the challenge to continue.
More training and resources on their own will not be sufficient to empower regulators to effectively address harms, Avramović warns. Technological solutions and a holistic approach are needed, he says.
National DPAs often have a single biometrics expert on staff, who must handle all complaints related to the technology.
3 paths and a framework of frameworks
Interoperability is typically achieved through a federated body or broker, wallet-based credential presentation, or direct API integration, Professor Carsten Maple of the Turing Institute says. These three paths come with different limitations. But all three require common trust arrangements between the parties to cover who is trusted, what data and protocols mean and set required levels of confidence. Identity records from two authorities (usually from different governments) must match and the relying party must be authorized to trust the data.
Austroads, ICAO and OpenID have each shown how particular types of evidence can cross borders to support specific claims.
At the same time, the SIDI Hub interoperability tests showed that work remains for systems to accommodate different national policies and architectures. The EU’s Digital Identity Wallet pilots have shown the need to test common specifications across different parties, and work by NOBID has shown that the right domestic record to authenticate against is not always clear (such as for people with the same name). LAC Digital Citizen showed the power of regional trust frameworks.
Later in the workshop, Maple presented the Standards-Aligned Assessment Framework for Interoperable Identity (SAAFII), which he describes as “a framework-of-frameworks” that can be used as a diagnostic tool.
During development of the tool, Turing researchers found that existing standards address much of the technical interoperability problem, while responsibility and governance remain key challenges. Technical sophistication can also conceal legal, institutional and trust gaps.
Data protection and intermediary layers
Data protection regulation can also act as trust infrastructure for interoperability, according to Ibukunoluwa Owa of the Nigerian Data Protection Commission and the Digital Impact Alliance.
Nigeria’s law states that data protection regulations apply to NINs wherever they are stored or processed, Owa says. That means interoperability must come with regulatory equivalence or some other mechanisms – binding corporate rules, certifications or codes of conduct, for example – in other jurisdictions.
Another approach is seen in the Smart Africa Data Exchange (SADX) pilot, which uses a federated trust platform owned by member states, explained Jeanne Yamfashije of Smart Africa. Benin, Ghana and Rwanda were selected for the pilot based on their readiness, but Yamfashije says the principal gap between them was trust, rather than technology.
To address that gap, behind the platform sit trust lists of certified solutions and rules set by SATA (Smart Africa Trust Alliance). These are enforced by a governance structure that includes working groups, the Smart Africa Secretariat, and monitoring and supervisory committees. The platform also allows data to be processed without being transmitted to or stored in another country.
Yamfashije identifies six key challenges: data protection approval, legal basis, assurance equivalence, national readiness, liability and redress, and coverage limitations.
The financial industry also wants to see KYC interoperability, and is therefore happy to help governments move in that direction, says Damola Owolade of financial services market facilitator Finmark Trust at the South African Development Community (SADC).
How exactly that will work in the SADC region is hard to say, however. Only a couple of digital ID wallets are available in the region, he says, and the consent mechanism built into Malawi’s wallet is a once-only process, so may not work with requirements of consent for a particular transaction.
Cross-border MOSIP through eSignet and OIDC chains
Beyond technical, legal and regulatory alignment, operational factors are important too. Security and availability are also required for effective interoperability, notes MOSIP VP and Head of Country Implementation Krishnan Rajagopalan.
He advises countries to remember the need for defined service-level expectations and incident escalation procedures.
Dr. Mirko Bottarelli explained how MOSIP ecosystems can connect to each other through eSignet by chaining OIDC flows, which avoids data privacy or scalability challenges that he says would otherwise make cross-border interactions impractical.
Bottarelli cites interoperability efforts by Mercosur, ECOWAS and Ukraine as evidence of significant progress this year. These efforts also highlight the importance of scalability, even as implementation continues to lag regulation.

articles.title: Thailand Watches US Midterms for Signals on Trade, Investment and Regional Stability - Thailand Business News
articles.summary: Thailand Watches US Midterms for Signals on Trade, Investment and Regional Stability  Thailand Business News
articles.full_text:
The outcome of the US midterm elections is being closely monitored across Asia, with potentially significant consequences for Thailand’s export-driven economy. The United States remains one of Thailand’s most important trading partners, with Thai exports to the US valued at approximately US$72.6 billion in 2025, led by electrical and electronic products, machinery, rubber products and vehicles.
For Thailand’s electronics sector, the stakes are particularly high. Electronics and electrical appliances have been the primary drivers of Thai export growth, supported by rising global demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors and data-centre technologies. Thai exports reached a record US$339.6 billion in 2025, with electronics playing a leading role. Any shift in US policy toward China, technology exports or semiconductor supply chains could directly affect and manufacturing activity in Thailand.
Thailand’s automotive and EV industries are also paying close attention. Motor vehicles and parts remain one of the country’s top export categories, accounting for more than 662 billion baht in exports during the first eight months of 2026. Future US trade measures and industrial policies could influence global production networks, investment decisions and demand for Thai-made vehicles and components.
Meanwhile, Thailand’s agricultural exporters, including rice, rubber and processed food producers, remain vulnerable to shifts in global trade patterns and tariff policies. Recent trade data show agricultural exports facing increasing competitive pressure despite strong performance in some processed food categories.
While the elections are a domestic US event, their impact could extend across global supply chains, trade flows and financial markets. For Thai , the key question is whether post-election policies support stable economic engagement with Asia or deepen strategic and economic divisions between the United States and China.

articles.title: Californian’s bill targets negligent pet boarding facilities after dog’s viral death - NBC News
articles.summary: Californian’s bill targets negligent pet boarding facilities after dog’s viral death  NBC NewsCalifornia congressman introduces legislation after 117 dead dogs recovered from rescue  KCRANorthern California Rep. Proposes New Pet Protections in Wake of Animal Welfare Probes  KQEDGallagher introduces Dunkin’s Law following tragic loss of family dog, horrific discovery at Northern California animal rescue  Lassen County NewsU.S. Rep. James Gallagher introduce...
articles.full_text:
After an influencer couple went viral in August when their dog died at a boarding facility, a congressman from California has introduced a bill to hold facilities more accountable when pets are harmed or killed.
Republican Rep. James Gallagher introduced the legislation, called “Dunkin’s Law,” named for the couple’s Bernese mountain dog. It would expand the state’s Animal Welfare Act “to provide for the protection of companion animals held or cared for at certain facilities,” according to the bill’s text.
The bill would classify pets as “sentient beings” and allow owners of pets that were harmed or killed at boarding and similar facilities to bring action against the facilities to recover damages and other lost expenses.
“There needs to be greater protections and teeth when something like this happens,” Gallagher told NBC News on Tuesday.
He said he hopes not only that the legislation protects families of pets that were hurt or that died but that it also ensures that no-kill shelters do not euthanize dogs and cats in “these horrific ways.”
“Make these people actually live up to their word, have accountability, especially for the kind of mistreatment and neglect that we’ve seen in these cases,” Gallagher said. “Hopefully, what it ultimately leads to is this doesn’t happen, that the disincentives are so strong that these guys really up their game and we don’t have bad actors.”
Two events prompted Gallagher to introduce the bill, he said in a release accompanying the announcement.
The first occurred in June, when Humboldt County sheriff’s investigators uncovered mass burial sites at a Northern California animal rescue facility. As part of an investigation into the shelter, officials recovered intact remains of 117 dogs, as well as other skeletal remains. Preliminary examinations of some of the dogs’ remains showed evidence of gunshot wounds.
“What investigators uncovered in Humboldt County is absolutely sickening,” Gallagher said in the release. “People entrusted these animals to a rescue believing they would be protected, only for authorities to discover more than a hundred dead dogs buried on the property.”
The second was in August, when Loud Luxury DJ Andrew Fedyk and his wife, Madeleine White Fedyk, said their dog Dunkin died at a board-and-train facility in Los Angeles.
Andrew Fedyk told NBC News in September that they chose to leave their two dogs, Dunkin and Poutine, at Smart Dogs Training, which is owned and operated by trainer Jeff Todd, while they went on vacation. He said that they found the business’ page online and that the flood of positive reviews prompted them to book their dogs, thinking basic leash training could help their already well-behaved pets.
But hours after they arrived in Europe, Fedyk said, Todd called to tell him Dunkin had died. Todd is alleged to have told Fedyk that the two dogs had been playing outside during a heat wave and that Dunkin died on the way to a separate boarding facility after “showing signs of heat exhaustion.”
Fedyk said Todd did not take Dunkin to a veterinarian. Poutine was OK and was later returned to the Fedyks.
Fedyk and his wife shared Dunkin’s story with their combined almost 2.5 million followers on social media, which he said prompted “a bunch of people” to reach out with individual stories about similar experiences.
Andrew Fedyk did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Todd did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday. When NBC News reached out in August, he declined to comment on Dunkin’s case.
In August, Los Angeles Animal Services said it was investigating the incident involving Dunkin. The agency did not immediately respond to an emailed request for more information sent Tuesday morning.
Los Angeles police declined to provide recent records for 911 calls and police reports relating to Todd’s address, citing an open investigation. The police department did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment sent Tuesday morning.
“Their heartbreaking story, along with the horrific discovery of more than 100 dead dogs at a Northern California rescue, exposes a serious gap in how we protect companion animals and hold those responsible for their care accountable,” Gallagher said of the Fedyks in an Instagram post announcing the legislation.
Gallagher said Dunkin’s story is why he is introducing this bill, calling it “legislation that would give pet owners a path to seek justice when their animals suffer harm or neglect at covered facilities, while strengthening accountability for unlawful euthanasia at rescues and shelters.”
Gallagher told NBC News on Tuesday that Dunkin’s case spurred the legislation, especially after he spoke to Fedyk and Madeleine White Fedyk, who he said expressed frustration and concern that there was no recourse — even though the couple does not fall within his constituency.
“Dunkin represents all of these dogs,” Gallagher said. “These have been some of the most horrendous examples, and we want to make sure it doesn’t ever happen again.”

articles.title: Countries Seek to Reduce Protein Import Dependence, Reshaping Global Trade - DatamarNews
articles.summary: Countries Seek to Reduce Protein Import Dependence, Reshaping Global Trade  DatamarNews
articles.full_text:
Oct, 27, 2026 Posted by Gabriel Malheiros
Week 202644
Governments around the world are restructuring agricultural and industrial policies to reduce their reliance on imported proteins, a shift that could reshape international trade flows in soybeans, animal feed, meat and food ingredients. Combining support for domestic production, investment in technology and greater control over supply chains, the trend is turning protein into a strategic national security resource rather than simply another commodity traded on international markets.
The shift has direct implications for Brazil. The country plays a central role in global soybean and animal protein supplies, but its export competitiveness now faces a new challenge: major buyers are increasingly willing to invest in producing domestically what they currently import.
The phenomenon, described as “protein nationalism” by political risk consultancy Eurasia Group in a report published in October 2026, extends beyond the threat of tariffs and quotas. It also raises the possibility of structural changes in demand, the emergence of subsidized competitors and growing competition for control over production and processing technologies.
The report identifies a convergence of geopolitical fragmentation, rising protein demand and greater government intervention in food production and trade. Under the scenario the consultancy considers most likely, countries will continue adopting measures to protect domestic supplies and increase production self-sufficiency, while trade restrictions become more widespread.
China at the Center of Protein Nationalism
China represents the most consequential shift for agricultural exporters. But Beijing is not alone. The United States is seeking to expand domestic beef production, the European Union wants to reduce its reliance on imported plant proteins used in animal feed, and India is investing in efforts to cut its dependence on imported pulses. Meanwhile, countries such as Denmark, the Netherlands, South Korea and Singapore are seeking to establish themselves in the alternative protein industry.
Although these initiatives reflect different national circumstances, they point in the same direction: governments want greater control over the origin, supply and cost of the proteins consumed by their populations and used by domestic industries.
China Pursues Self-Sufficiency and Could Reduce Imports
China poses the greatest potential threat to traditional protein suppliers. Having become the world’s largest importer of meat, dairy products and animal feed, the country is seeking to reduce its exposure to international markets, increase domestic productivity and develop technologies that would allow it to replace imports and eventually expand into export markets.
China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, covering 2026–2030, places food security among the country’s highest national priorities, alongside defense. Its strategy includes developing genetically modified seeds, expanding cultivated areas, improving feed production efficiency and investing in precision fermentation, cellular agriculture, amino acids and biomanufacturing.
The objective is not necessarily to eliminate imports in the short term, but to reduce China’s vulnerability to foreign suppliers and fluctuations in international trade. In May 2026, a Reuters analysis had already suggested that productivity gains and declining reliance on imported animal feed could bring about structural changes in Chinese demand for agricultural products, with particularly significant implications for Brazil and the United States.
For Brazil, the issue is especially sensitive because China is a major destination for Brazilian soybean and beef exports. If the Asian country succeeds in producing more animal protein while using fewer imported inputs, its demand for foreign soybeans and soybean meal could decline even as domestic meat consumption continues to grow.
Seaborne trade data obtained by Datamar illustrate the scale of the downturn: beef shipments to China fell 81% in July compared with the previous month. The chart below provides a detailed view of the volumes recorded:
Beef Exports to China | Jan 2024 – Aug 2026 | TEUs
Source: DataLiner – explore our trade data
There is, however, an important distinction between reducing dependence on imports and eliminating them altogether. China’s ability to replace foreign suppliers will depend on agricultural productivity, land and water availability, production costs and the pace of technological adoption. Eurasia Group projects a decline in Chinese soybean and animal feed purchases beginning in 2027, although it does not quantify the potential impact on Brazilian export volumes.
Competition presents a second risk. In addition to seeking to replace products currently imported, China intends to expand its exports of poultry meat, dairy products, eggs and aquatic products. If successful, this strategy could bring Chinese suppliers into direct competition with established exporters, supported by industrial policies and government investment.
U.S. Supports Domestic Cattle Industry While Relying on Imports to Contain Prices
In the United States, protein sovereignty is taking a different form. The government is seeking to rebuild domestic beef production while also addressing the impact of insufficient supplies on consumer prices.
The U.S. cattle herd is at its lowest level in 75 years, according to Eurasia Group and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). To encourage production, the government has introduced measures to support cattle ranchers, including loan guarantees, expanded access to grazing land and increased oversight of major meatpacking companies.
At the same time, Washington has expanded access for foreign beef suppliers in an effort to ease domestic prices. A measure that took effect in September 2026 temporarily increased the lower-tariff import quota for certain lean beef products by an additional 300,000 metric tonnes, with Brazil expected to be a major beneficiary.
This apparent contradiction illustrates the dilemma facing governments pursuing food sovereignty. Expanding domestic production is a long-term objective, but it does not immediately resolve supply shortages. Until production capacity responds, imports may remain necessary to contain inflation and ensure adequate supplies.
The episode also shows how trade policy can serve domestic interests while strengthening diplomatic relationships. The U.S. government has expanded trade benefits for Argentina, for example, in a strategy that Eurasia Group associates with the political relationship between Donald Trump and Javier Milei.
For Brazilian exporters, this means market access may depend not only on prices and competitiveness but also on political decisions, bilateral negotiations and the supply requirements of importing countries.
European Union Seeks to Reduce Dependence on Imported Soybeans
The European Union has also begun treating protein supplies as a matter of strategic autonomy. In July 2026, the European Commission presented a plan to strengthen the resilience and autonomy of Europe’s protein supply system, focusing on diversifying production and reducing external dependencies.
The objective is to expand European production of plant-based proteins used in both human food and animal feed. The plan calls for incentives to diversify crops, investment in research and innovation, and stronger processing supply chains.
Reliance on imported inputs is considered a vulnerability because it exposes European livestock production to price fluctuations, logistics disruptions and geopolitical tensions. The problem extends beyond soybeans, as fertilizers and energy are also critical inputs for the supply chain.
Europe faces natural and economic constraints that limit its ability to expand certain crops on the same scale as major exporters in the Americas. According to Eurasia Group, reducing dependence will therefore require gradual changes in production, incentives for farmers and the development of alternative protein sources.
For Brazil, the potential consequence is greater competition in the European market for animal feed ingredients. This does not mean that the EU will stop importing Brazilian soybeans, but rather that it intends to broaden its sourcing options and reduce exposure to a limited group of suppliers.
India Invests in Replacing Pulse Imports
India is also pursuing greater self-sufficiency through a roughly $1.3 billion program aimed at reducing its dependence on imported pulses, including supplies from Canada and Australia. The initiative covers the 2025–26 to 2030–31 period, with the goal of achieving self-sufficiency in pulse production by the end of the program.
The initiative illustrates how protein sovereignty extends beyond meat. Pulses, protein-rich grains and animal feed ingredients are also considered strategic because they influence dietary costs, food security and dependence on international trade.
In heavily populated countries, exposure to high international prices can have significant economic and political consequences. Encouraging domestic production therefore becomes a means of reducing vulnerability to external shocks, although replacing imports depends on productivity, land availability, farm profitability and weather conditions.
Technology Competition Extends Beyond Conventional Livestock Production
The drive for self-sufficiency is not limited to producing more meat, milk or eggs. Some governments are seeking to gain control over technologies that could fundamentally change the structure of the protein market.
The Netherlands, Denmark, the United Kingdom, South Korea and Singapore are investing in research, development and production of plant-based proteins, fermentation-derived ingredients and cultivated meat. China has also incorporated these technologies into its food security strategy.
The motivation is both economic and geopolitical. Control over industrial p

articles.title: EU accepts Temu’s action plan to remedy Digital Services Act breaches following €200m penalty - The News International
articles.summary: EU accepts Temu’s action plan to remedy Digital Services Act breaches following €200m penalty  The News International
articles.full_text:
Under a newly approved compliance roadmap, the cross-border e-commerce giant must overhaul its risk assessment protocols and crack down on illegal products within four months
The European Commission has officially accepted a corrective compliance roadmap submitted by cross-border e-commerce platform Temu.
The move follows a landmark €200 million fine levied against the company over systemic failures to curb the widespread sale of counterfeit, unsafe, and illegal products under the European Union's strict Digital Services Act (DSA).
The plan focuses on five measures to remedy the breach, and Temu now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment, the EU regulator, said in a statement.
The five-point action plan:
Under the newly accepted framework, Temu is legally bound to overhaul its backend operations across five critical pillars such as:
Targeted risk analysis:
Factoring the specific vulnerabilities of its high-volume discount marketplace model into security evaluations.
Mitigation metrics:
Establishing verifiable benchmarks to track how effectively illicit listings are flagged and eliminated.
Content moderation audits:
Upgrading automated and human review systems that screen for banned merchandise.
Algorithmic accountability:
Scrutinizing recommendation engines to ensure platform algorithms do not actively promote unsafe or illegal items.
Seller exploitation defenses:
Closing loopholes that bad-faith merchants use to disguise or elevate problematic listings.
The Commission had imposed a €200 million ($224.08 million) fine on Temu in May for not doing enough to stop the sale of illegal products.
A spokesperson for Temu, which is owned by PDD Holdings, said it welcomed the Commission's approval of its plan under which the company will have to assess possible shortcomings of its content moderation system, among other steps.
Temu, along with Shein and other ecommerce platforms, has been hit by the EU imposing €3 fees on low-value ecommerce packages since the start of July.
Parcels worth less than €150 previously entered the bloc duty-free.
Regulators previously found that Temu's platform safeguards and risk assessment procedures were fundamentally inadequate, allowing dangerous goods such as non-compliant electrical chargers and children's toys exceeding chemical safety limits—to easily reach European consumers.

articles.title: The Trump admin said energy costs were a small price to pay in Iran war, but U.S. consumers are paying nearly 8x more than anyone else in fuel costs - Fortune
articles.summary: The Trump admin said energy costs were a small price to pay in Iran war, but U.S. consumers are paying nearly 8x more than anyone else in fuel costs  FortuneHow Expensive is Gasoline Where You Live?  WSJUS paying most for Hormuz oil shock with world’s largest fuel bill  Centre for Research on Energy and Clean AirAmerica's affordability crisis: The price of war is in everything we buy  The Miami Times20 states have seen their gas prices increase more than 5...
articles.full_text:
The Iran war continues to weigh on Americans’ wallets, and it’s costing them more in increased fuel costs than consumers in any other country in the world, new data finds. As President Donald Trump argues the cost of the war will be justified with economic prosperity, his administration may be pushing policies making the problem worse.
U.S. consumers have paid an average of $471 more in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran war in February, according to a report published on Monday by Finland-based nonprofit research institute Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). That’s nearly eight times greater than the average of about $60 in increased energy costs per person globally. As a country, the U.S. has spent $160 billion total on increased fuel costs since the beginning of the war, with China following at $54 billion, and Canada coming in third at $17 billion.
The Iran war has cost U.S. households about $2,000, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, a sum that includes both soaring prices at the gas pump as well as increased airfares and inflation as a result of increased transportation expenses and supply-chain shuffles over the last seven months of Middle East turmoil.
Trump has repeatedly tried to assuage Americans’ anxieties about increased costs associated with the war. At a rally in North Carolina in September, the president downplayed affordability concerns. He has argued the war is necessary to prevent Iran from attaining nuclear weapons, and that the U.S. is making a “freaking fortune” as a result of increased energy production.
“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done,” Trump said last month of fuel costs, which have now topped $4.26 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the war. “Remember that.”
The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.
Why are fuel costs for Americans higher than in the rest of the world?
To be sure, the Iran war did not create the conditions under which American consumers in particular are paying higher energy costs. While global supply strains have increased fuel prices globally, the outsize impact on U.S. consumers is a result of an American economy and culture structured around oil.
“If you compare the U.S. with countries in Europe with similar levels of income, you can really see the effect of decades of lower prices for fuel and less emphasis on sustainable transportation,” CREA cofounder and report author Lauri Myllyvirta told Fortune. “Undoing that, of course, takes quite a bit of time and effort.”
The U.S. is heavily exposed to higher fuel costs in part because it is beholden to global market rates, a result of it still having to trade for heavy oil despite being a major diesel producer. But the heavier energy burden on American consumers is mostly because of the country’s reliance on oil over other sustainable means of energy, CREA argued.
The U.S. has less electric-vehicle adoption than other countries. And less efficient gas-powered cars travel farther on American roads compared to other countries, meaning American consumers simply burn more fuel than consumers in other countries, the report said. CREA found a positive correlation between countries with the greatest EV market share—Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands, and Belgium—and fuel cost savings per person.
Across the world, EV sales have surged as fuel costs have increased. In Denmark, for example, EVs made up 81% of new-vehicle sales in the first eight months of 2026. Nearly all new-vehicle sales in Norway over the same period were EVs, and 57% of new-vehicle sales in China were all-electric. Some European countries such as Germany saw a decrease in gas and diesel demand in 2026.
By comparison, only 7.3% of new-vehicle sales in the U.S. over that span were plug-in EVs, and the report found that American drivers who made the switch to eclectic cars saw only a $17 increase in charging costs since early March as a result of electricity price increases.
How could Trump’s policies still increase fuel costs for Americans?
Myllyvirta suggested this pattern is primed to continue. A series of U.S. policy changes has disincentivized Americans from purchasing EVs and automakers from building fuel efficient vehicles.
The Trump administration ended a $7,500 tax credit on new EVs in September 2025 it claimed would devastate the auto industry. Analysts have cited the end of the incentive as the reason EV demand flattened in the U.S., and the reason why companies like Ford rolled back production on all-electric cars in favor of hybrid vehicles.
Last month, Trump released new fuel economy standards, loosening Biden-era regulatory requirements for fuel efficiency to mitigate pollution—a move the president said would make cars more affordable, but that environmentalists argued would drive up fuel costs and cancel out any vehicle savings.
According to Myllyvirta, increased fuel costs for Americans are poised to continue, even if the war ends. While energy prices will level out once this conflict is over, the reliance on gas-powered cars will mean a repetition of this cycle during the next energy shock.
“The only certainty is volatility,” he said. “Prices are going to come down, and then there are going to be new shocks. And as long as the reliance on oil continues, that cycle is going to play out with effects on consumers, with effects on inflation and economic policy.”
