articles.title: EU Commission accepts Temu’s action plan to address DSA breach - Digital Watch Observatory
articles.summary: EU Commission accepts Temu’s action plan to address DSA breach  Digital Watch Observatory
articles.full_text:
Temu must review its content moderation, recommendation algorithms and exposure to manipulation by sellers and other users.
The European Commission has accepted Temu’s action plan to remedy an infringement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) concerning its assessment of risks linked to illegal products sold through its platform. Announced on 26 October 2026, the decision follows a finding that Temu failed to adequately assess the systemic risks associated with illegal product listings. The plan was submitted in August and sets out five corrective measures intended to improve how the company identifies, evaluates and mitigates these risks.
Under the five point plan, i) Temu has committed to conducting a platform-specific risk assessment using reliable and up-to-date information. ii) It will also establish metrics and indicators to evaluate the effectiveness of measures intended to reduce the circulation of illegal products. iii) The company must assess potential weaknesses in its proactive content moderation system, including automated detection, manual reviews, feedback mechanisms and resource allocation, and examine how these limitations could affect the products recommended to users.
The remaining measures focus iv) on the role of algorithmic recommendation systems and possible manipulation of the platform. Lastly, it must v) analyse whether its recommender systems could amplify the distribution of illegal product listings and use relevant, reliable metrics in that assessment. As part of the last point, Temu must also investigate how traders and other users might exploit the platform’s features to spread potentially illegal listings more widely. The company has four months to implement the action plan and must conduct an interim risk assessment covering a six-month period ending on 30 November 2026.
The European Commission consulted the Board for Digital Services on the proposed measures. In its opinion, the Board considered the changes partially adequate and said the plan lacked sufficient detail to establish fully whether it addressed the infringement. The Commission said it had taken this assessment into account and clarified key requirements Temu must follow during implementation. The Commission will continue supervising the process, particularly in areas where additional information or explanation was considered necessary.
Temu has also committed to an external, independent audit of the measures. It must submit the audit report to the Commission within four months of implementing the plan. If the auditor makes recommendations, Temu has to report back within one month on how those recommendations have been addressed. The decision follows a €200 million fine imposed by the Commission in May 2026 after it confirmed that Temu had failed to meet its DSA risk assessment obligations.
Why does it matter?
This important step in the enforcement of the DSA reflects how the EU expects online intermediary services to follow through with design changes to ensure a high level of protection for consumers in the Union.

articles.title: Australian Labor spent AU$2.6M ousting 2 Greens rivals from parliament - Politico
articles.summary: Australian Labor spent AU$2.6M ousting 2 Greens rivals from parliament  Politico
articles.full_text:
CANBERRA — The Labor Party spent AU$1.3 million in each of two inner-city Brisbane seats held by the Greens, including its successful bid to oust the prime minister’s antagonist, Max Chandler-Mather, from parliament.
Just months after the Albanese government legislated an electoral spending cap of $800,000 per seat, but before the new law took effect, Labor spent half a million dollars more than that to unseat Chandler-Mather from his Griffith seat. The party matched that spending to defeat Stephen Bates in the neighboring seat of Brisbane.
The new statistics on Labor’s campaign spending are contained in the Commonwealth’s defense to a legal challenge by two former independent members of parliament against the spending and donation caps, obtained from the High Court by POLITICO.
In February 2025, Labor and the Coalition combined to pass a bill to cap political donations, increase public funding and limit electoral expenditure, measures that will commence in 2027.

articles.title: Defence supply chain resilience in Europe - World Economic Forum
articles.summary: Defence supply chain resilience in Europe  World Economic Forum
articles.full_text:
- Europe’s increased defence investment creates an opportunity to rebuild the industrial foundations on which those capabilities depend.
In 2025, defence spending by EU Member States reached €418 billion, a 20% increase on the previous year. The European Defence Agency projects that it will rise to €454 billion in 2026.
Europe is spending more on defence than ever before. But this cannot guarantee access to the components, materials and manufacturing capacity on which defence readiness depends. Increased budgets must translate into the industrial capacity needed to deliver, maintain and replenish the capabilities Europe’s armed forces require.
This means looking beyond procurement and considering how to secure the industrial foundations of the region’s defence capabilities. Europe should explore rebuilding selected manufacturing capabilities at home, strengthening industrial supply chains with trusted partners and making better use of materials and components that are already in circulation.
Defence readiness as industrial supply chain resilience
Modern defence systems depend on complex supply chains spanning batteries, electronics, semiconductors, specialized metals and advanced manufacturing. Even equipment assembled in Europe can rely on critical inputs produced or processed elsewhere.
The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 highlights the risks created by concentrated supply chains and export controls that affect both critical minerals and the technologies used to process them. Such vulnerabilities extend beyond energy technologies to the broader industrial ecosystem, including advanced manufacturing and defence.
Recognizing this challenge, the European Commission’s Readiness Roadmap 2030 identifies securing defence supply chains and reducing critical dependencies in raw materials and other inputs as priorities.
The question is not simply whether Europe can afford to buy the equipment it needs. The industrial ecosystem must be able to deliver it at scale, maintain it over time and replenish supplies when demand rises or external supply chains are disrupted.
Strategic autonomy does not mean self-sufficiency
Europe cannot realistically produce every component or process every raw material it needs within its borders. Nor would complete self-sufficiency necessarily be economically sensible. The objective should instead be to distinguish between dependencies that must be reduced, those that can be diversified and those that can be managed through cooperation with trusted partners. This requires a more deliberate approach to industrial policy.
Some strategically critical capabilities may need to be developed or expanded within Europe. Others can be secured through partnerships with countries that share compatible security interests, supported by diversified sourcing, coordinated investment and reliable long-term supply arrangements.
Cooperation also matters within Europe itself. The Commission’s roadmap sets objectives for greater joint procurement and increased investment in the European defence technological and industrial base. NATO’s updated Defence Production Action Plan similarly emphasises demand aggregation, industrial capacity and the security of critical supply chains.
This is an opportunity to build networks of complementary industrial capabilities rather than simply reproduce every capability in every country. But there is another dimension to resilience that deserves greater attention: reducing the need for new materials and components in the first place.
Circularity across industrial supply chains
Industrial resilience is usually discussed in terms of where materials are extracted, components are manufactured and products are assembled. Less attention is given to what happens throughout subsequent lifecycles.
Repair and refurbishment can extend the useful life of equipment and reduce the need for replacement. Where technically and operationally appropriate, component recovery can preserve value and reduce demand for new parts. Recycling can return strategic materials from batteries, electronics and other products to productive use.
These approaches cannot eliminate Europe’s dependence on primary raw materials, and recovery is not always technically or economically feasible. Defence applications also require stringent standards for safety, reliability, traceability and information security.
Nevertheless, the potential is significant. The IEA identifies recycling as an increasingly important contributor to future mineral supply, while highlighting the need for investment in collection and processing infrastructure. For Europe, this suggests that resource recovery should be considered alongside mining, processing, manufacturing and procurement in strategic supply-chain planning.
The relevant infrastructure need not serve defence alone. Where requirements overlap, investment in materials processing, electronics recovery, battery recycling and specialized manufacturing can support a wider industrial ecosystem. This means identifying where shared civilian and military applications can strengthen resilience for both.
There are three priorities for policymakers:
1. Map strategic dependencies across entire supply chains
Governments should identify critical materials, components and processing capabilities, including upstream dependencies that may not be visible in direct supplier relationships.
This would help distinguish where domestic capacity is essential, where trusted partnerships offer greater resilience and where substitution or recovery could reduce exposure.
2. Make lifecycle resilience part of industrial and procurement policy
Procurement decisions should consider not only acquisition costs and delivery times, but also maintainability, repairability, component availability and access to replacement materials.
Predictable demand and coordinated procurement can help give industry the confidence to invest in the capabilities required.
3. Integrate circularity into strategic-material planning
Governments and industry should identify opportunities to extend equipment lifetimes, recover usable components and return valuable materials to supply chains.
This would require investment in appropriate infrastructure, technical standards and traceability, alongside security safeguards and realistic assessments of recovery potential.
Circularity cannot replace secure sourcing or new production capacity, just as domestic manufacturing cannot eliminate every external dependency. Their value lies in combining them into a coherent resilience strategy.
Industrial supply chain readiness in Europe
Europe’s increased defence investment creates an opportunity to strengthen more than its immediate military capabilities. It can also help rebuild the industrial foundations on which those capabilities depend.
That means deciding what Europe must produce itself, what it can secure through trusted partners and how it can retain and recover more of the materials and components already available.
And Europe does not have to manufacture everything within its borders. Strategic autonomy means taking a deliberate approach to managing industrial supply chain dependencies and sustaining critical capabilities when conditions change.
The measure of defence readiness is not simply what Europe can buy today, but what its industrial system can continue to deliver tomorrow.

articles.title: CPI | Merger Control in the Absence of FDI Screening in Latin America - PYMNTS.com
articles.summary: CPI | Merger Control in the Absence of FDI Screening in Latin America  PYMNTS.com
articles.full_text:
By: Mariana Camacho Ordóñez[1] & Francesca Chocano Villanueva[2]
I. Introduction
Most Latin American countries review foreign acquisitions for their effects on competition, but few have dedicated foreign direct investment (FDI) screening mechanisms to assess their national security implications. In this setting, competition authorities may face demands to address concerns about strategic assets, critical inputs, or foreign state influence through merger review, even where those concerns fall outside their statutory mandate.
This article asks three related questions: whether merger control performs a security-screening function in practice where no dedicated screening regime exists; whether competition authorities may lawfully perform that function; and, perhaps most importantly, whether they should. It addresses these questions through a brief analysis of ten merger reviews of transactions involving Chinese state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Peru between 2010 and 2025.
The ten reviews show varying scrutiny of state ownership, but no decisions resting on national security as an independent ground. The cases also point to a less visible consequence of the way authorities define SOE groups: a finding of a single economic unit adopted to assess an acquisition may later be invoked to place coordination among commonly owned enterprises outside of cartel enforcement.
The article makes three contributions: (i) it provides decision-based comparative evidence from a region that has received little attention in comparative works on the interaction between FDI screening and merger control;[3] (ii) it proposes a classification and a sufficiency test that separate competition remedies with wider protective effects from security screening conducted through merger control; and (iii) it examines the enforcement consequences of SOE group definitions. Section II distinguishes the two review functions, Section III sets out the method, Section IV presents the national findings, Section V assesses the reach of merger control, Section VI turns to findings of a single economic unit, and finally Section VII discusses Mexico’s 2026 proposal.
II. Merger Control and FDI Screening in Latin America
Merger control asks whether a transaction is likely to substantially lessen competition. FDI screening asks whether a foreign investment threatens national security or another essential interest of the State. Both may apply to the same transaction and examine the same ownership chain, and each answers its own legal question. A clearance on competition grounds leaves the security risk unassessed, and a security approval leaves the competitive effects unassessed.[4]
Jurisdictions that screen investment on security grounds do so under an express legal basis. The United States built its review system through successive statutes administered by CFIUS, the European Union coordinates national screening under Regulation (EU) 2019/452, and the United Kingdom adopted a standalone regime in the National Security and Investment Act 2021. Some systems also allow for public-interest considerations within merger procedures, but that power rests on statute, and the absence of a separate screening regime cannot supply it.
Latin America followed a different path. Merger control spread across the region, while dedicated security screening did not. Foreign ownership limits, border restrictions, and sectoral authorizations exist, while their coverage varies. Peru’s Constitution bars foreigners from acquiring energy sources and other assets within fifty kilometers of the borders, subject to exceptions declared by supreme decree,[5] while its merger-control law aims to promote effective competition and economic efficiency for consumers’ benefit.[6] Neither Peru, Chile, nor Brazil has a general procedure for screening foreign investment on security grounds. Mexico’s Foreign Investment Law empowers the National Foreign Investment Commission (CNIE) to block acquisitions on national security grounds, but provides no procedure, thresholds, or criteria for doing so.[7] Sectoral authorizations, such as approval for a change of control in an electricity concession, look at compliance with the sector’s regulatory regime; whether they also assess the security implications of foreign ownership depends on the sector and its applicable rules.
Sectoral regulators and, in Mexico, the CNIE are gatekeepers too, but the former decide within their own regulatory remit and the latter has no procedure. Where pre-closing merger review is mandatory, the competition authority may therefore become the most visible gatekeeper, which explains the pressure placed on it, while the scope of its mandate remains set by its statute.
III. Methodology and Analytical Framework
Our analysis comprises ten reviews of acquisitions by Chinese SOEs or their subsidiaries, two in each jurisdiction (Table 1). The eight reviews in Brazil, Chile, Mexico and Peru were examined through the authorities’ published decisions. The Argentine account draws on the competition commission’s opinion in Sinopec/Occidental–Vintage and principally on research summaries in ChemChina/Syngenta. A complaint filed with Brazil’s competition authority in 2025 provides contextual evidence for the pressure being placed on merger review.
Table 1. Merger reviews examined
| Country | Transaction | Proceeding | Year | Outcome | Category | 
| Brazil | State Grid / CPFL Energia | AC 08700.006319/2016-39 | 2016 | Unconditional | Competition-only (provisional) | 
| Brazil | CTG / Duke Energy’s Brazilian assets | AC 08700.007003/2016-64 | 2016 | Unconditional | Competition-only (provisional) | 
| Argentina | Sinopec / Occidental–Vintage | Conc. 683 | 2014 | Unconditional | Competition-only | 
| Argentina | ChemChina / Syngenta | Conc. 1465 | 2021 | Unconditional | Competition-only | 
| Chile | State Grid / Chilquinta–Eletrans | F219-2019 | 2020 | Unconditional | Competition-only | 
| Chile | State Grid / CGE | F255-2020 | 2021 | Unconditional | Competition-only; express boundary | 
| Mexico | ChemChina / Syngenta | CNT-083-2016 | 2017 | Conditional | Legitimate grey zone | 
| Mexico | CTG–Kinich / solar assets | CNT-152-2021 | 2022 | Unconditional | Competition-only (provisional) | 
| Peru | CYPI / Luz del Sur | 007-2020/CLC | 2020 | Conditional | Legitimate grey zone | 
| Peru | CSGI / Enel Distribución and Enel X | 014-2024/CLC | 2024 | Conditional | Legitimate grey zone | 
The comparative analysis uses three categories. ‘Competition-only review’ covers decisions grounded in competition law, including those that examine state ownership because it affects control or incentives. ‘Legitimate grey zones’ cover competition remedies that also address part of a wider investment concern without exceeding the authority’s mandate. ‘Off-label antitrust’ covers the use of merger control to pursue security or other objectives the competition mandate does not support. The first label differs from the OECD’s concept of competitive neutrality, which concerns a level playing field between state-owned and private enterprises.[8] A procurement obligation that prevents a distributor from favoring affiliated generators belongs in the grey zone if it also reduces dependence on those generators; the same obligation imposed only to limit a foreign state’s influence over supply would be off-label.
This classification turns on one question: would the stated justification for intervention remain legally sufficient without the identified risk to competition? If the measure depends on a competition rationale, any security benefit is overlap. If national security supplies independent grounds for action, the authority is screening and its legal basis must be examined. The test applies to documented reasoning and makes no claim about officials’ motives.
The design has limits. Silence on national security leaves open the question of whether a risk was examined and rejected, and whether any other institution considered it. The two Brazilian decisions, adopted under a summary procedure, contain limited discussion of their reasoning, and redactions limit the public version of one Mexican decision; the classification for these cases is provisional. Colombia was considered at the design stage but is not included because no merger decision by the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio concerning an acquisition by a Chinese SOE was identified for the period. The article considers no acquisitions by other state-owned investors or by privately owned Chinese firms, so it cannot separate the effect of nationality from that of state ownership. Finally, all ten transactions were authorized, and abandoned or unnotified transactions fall outside the sample.
IV. Findings from the National Merger Reviews
A. Brazil
CADE’s General Superintendence cleared State Grid’s acquisition of CPFL Energia and China Three Gorges’ purchase of Duke Energy’s Brazilian generation assets in 2016, without restrictions and under the summary procedure.[9][10] The CPFL transaction, worth about USD 4.5 billion, was among the largest Chinese investments in Brazil. The Duke assets, valued at about USD 1.2 billion, comprised ten hydroelectric plants. In both decisions, Chinese state ownership serves to identify the purchasers and plays no further role in the standard applied. The CPFL transaction also required authorization from ANEEL, the electricity regulator, granted in December 2016 as a sectoral approval of the change of control in a regulated concession. Neither decision asks whether SASAC could coordinate the conduct of otherwise separate Chinese enterprises, and nothing in them presents sectoral regulation as an assurance on national security. In 2025, Corex Holding asked CADE to review MMG’s proposed acquisition of Anglo American’s Brazilian nickel business, invoking common Chinese state control, supply-chain vulnerability, and Brazil’s policy on strategic minerals.[11] T

articles.summary: Why reported Khamenei call for end to 'neither war nor peace' moved markets - a bit  MorningstarOil prices fall after Iran supreme leader and top security official discuss conditions to end war  CNBCIran’s Khamenei Reiterates Conditions for Ending War With US  Bloomberg.comIran security chief meets Supreme Leader after talks with Mecca pact countries  ReutersWhy reported Khamenei call for end to ‘neither war nor peace’ moved markets — a bit  Mark...
articles.full_text:
By Steve Goldstein
This handout picture provided by the Iranian presidency shows (R to L) Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei during their meeting with Saudi Arabia's Defence Minister, Pakistan's army chief, and Turkey's intelligence chief in Tehran on October 26, 2026.
To the outside world, it's not even clear that Mojtaba Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, is alive.
But whether he is or not, Iranian news agencies reported on a meeting Khamenei had with Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the country's Supreme National Security Council, in which he reportedly called to bring "the current state of neither war nor peace to an end."
To be clear, the remarks indicated that the deal would have to be done on Iran's terms. One clause, according to the Islamic Republic News Agency, is "safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz." That may not fly with the Trump administration that has been escorting tankers, at great cost and peril, through the contested waterway.
The word "nuclear" doesn't come up once in IRNA's reporting. So there's a long way to go between these comments and any sort of U.S.-Iran deal.
That said, Khamenei's desire to end the conflict has not previously been articulated. And it comes after a four-way meeting between Iranian, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials that also was held on Tuesday.
U.S. stock-market futures moved to session highs, though not massively, with the S&P 500 contract (ES00) recently up 0.3%. Oil futures (CL00) fell by 1%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury BX:TMUBMUSD10Y eased by 1 basis point.
-Steve Goldstein

articles.title: Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress  Euronews.comRussian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones have nearly 60% interception rate – General Staff says  UkrinformUkraine’s Drones Have Eliminated or Wounded an Army of 300,000 Russians in Less Than a Year  UNITED24 MediaUkraine Downs 257 Russian Targets, Including 2 Ballistic Missiles and 255 Drones in Overnight Attack  Kyiv PostWith Kyiv’s air defense ...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

articles.title: Tata Motors Swallows Iveco for €3.9 Billion, Adding a Formidable Rival to Chinese Commercial Vehicle Makers Going Global - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Tata Motors Swallows Iveco for €3.9 Billion, Adding a Formidable Rival to Chinese Commercial Vehicle Makers Going Global  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
On October 27, preliminary results disclosed by the Italian Stock Exchange showed that Tata Motors' tender offer for Iveco Group had received sufficient shareholder acceptances, with shares tendered representing 89.42% of ordinary share capital excluding treasury shares, clearing the 80% threshold required for the deal. If the final results and remaining closing conditions are confirmed, the two sides plan to complete payment and settlement on October 30.
The deal was first announced in July 2025 and has taken about 15 months, delayed by regulatory approvals and met with resistance from some minority shareholders over the offer price. Tata has raised its per-share offer from €14.1 to €14.4 (about $16). Assuming full acceptance, the maximum cash consideration is approximately €3.906 billion (about $4.4 billion); on an enterprise value basis, the deal is worth about $4.5 billion.
Iveco's defense business was previously sold to Leonardo. The assets Tata is taking over include trucks, buses, FPT Powertrain and the financial services segment. The combined commercial vehicle businesses would sell more than 540,000 vehicles a year, with combined revenue exceeding $25 billion.
Deal Structure and Business Footprint
Geographically, about half of the combined group's sales would come from Europe, with India at 35% and the Americas at 15%. Iveco has deep roots in the European market and is also Latin America's third-largest commercial vehicle manufacturer; Tata Motors has a more mature presence in India and parts of Africa, and the two sides' distribution networks in markets such as West Asia are complementary.
On the product side, Iveco already has mature capabilities in niches such as heavy mining trucks and tractor-trailers—product lines where Tata has yet to achieve scale.
| Key Deal Data | Figure | 
|---|---|
| Shares tendered (excluding treasury shares) | 89.42% | 
| Minimum acceptance threshold for closing | 80% | 
| Offer price per share | €14.4 (previously €14.1) | 
| Maximum cash consideration | Approximately €3.906 billion | 
| Enterprise value | Approximately $4.5 billion | 
| Combined annual sales volume | More than 540,000 vehicles | 
| Combined annual revenue | More than $25 billion | 
Note: The acceptance ratio reflects preliminary results of the first-round offer on October 27; final figures are subject to official announcement.
Cost-Cutting Logic and Integration Constraints
In explaining the integration plan to investors, Tata proposed controlling costs through joint procurement, expanding low-cost sourcing, and consolidating some electrification, emissions and intelligent-vehicle R&D spending. Analysts tracking the deal noted that about 40% of the two companies' R&D budgets go to similar projects, leaving room to cut duplicate spending after integration. Tata management believes the synergies from the acquisition could exceed those from its 2008 purchase of Jaguar Land Rover.
However, the cost benefits will not materialize immediately. Iveco's 2024 revenue was €15.3 billion (about $17.1 billion), down 4% year on year, with about three-quarters coming from Europe, where its business shrank about 7% that year. In the second quarter of this year, Iveco's revenue rose 7.3% year on year, but adjusted EBIT fell to €131 million (about $146.1 million) from €171 million (about $190.7 million) a year earlier. The company attributed part of the profit pressure to product quality investment and bus rework costs, saying the rework has been completed and profitability will gradually recover in the second half.
The formal offer also carries two-year non-financial commitments: retaining Iveco's main brands, its Turin headquarters and operating structure, with no major restructuring or plant closures for two years. That means Tata must squeeze out synergies while maintaining the existing manufacturing system, and how much it can save through procurement and R&D integration will directly determine the deal's return.
On personnel, Tata Sons Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran, Jaguar Land Rover CEO P.B. Balaji and Tata Motors Managing Director Girish Wagh are among those set to join Iveco's board. Wagh has proposed using Iveco's distribution network to bring Tata trucks into Latin America and introducing some Iveco products into the Indian market; these arrangements still await implementation after closing.
New Variable for Chinese Commercial Vehicle Makers Going Global
Latin America is the most direct window for observing the deal's spillover effects. Foton Motor is accelerating its expansion in Brazil, with 1,745 local registrations in the first half of this year, up 138% year on year; the company has started a truck assembly line in Rio Grande do Sul and operates a parts distribution center in Itajaí. Local production and after-sales investment need sales growth to absorb them gradually, and if Tata can plug its products directly into Iveco's ready-made channels and service system, the new group could expand in Latin America without the expense of building a network from scratch—and combined with procurement and R&D cost cuts, its room for price adjustments could widen.
Competition in Europe's bus market is more direct. According to statistics from DVV cited by industry outlet Sustainable Bus, in the first half of this year, in the category of battery-electric buses over 8 tons across markets including the EU and the UK, Yutong Bus registered 1,636 units, while Iveco and Heuliez combined registered 1,156—the two are already competing for the same wave of electrification renewal demand.
European customers buying buses often sign contracts bundling vehicles with multi-year service. Iveco's 2024 order from Rome's ATAC, for example, covered 411 electric buses plus ten years of full-service maintenance, with local dealers providing repair workshops and on-site support. If vehicle manufacturing costs fall, Iveco would have more room to maneuver on contract pricing while keeping existing service arrangements intact.
Yutong is also shoring up its service capabilities. In September this year, it opened its first comprehensive service center in Europe, in Stokke, Norway, combining delivery, repair, parts and training in one location, equipped with facilities to support mandatory local annual inspections. China's electric bus development and manufacturing capabilities have already helped Yutong win orders; future service investment will determine whether these vehicles can keep operating in Europe and influence customers' choices in the next procurement round.
In light commercial vehicles, Iveco can also win customers through the RENTIVE long-term rental program offered by IVECO CAPITAL, which bundles vehicles, equipment, maintenance and roadside assistance, with customers comparing total usage costs over the contract term. Once manufacturing costs decline, Iveco's room to adjust pricing for the entire package opens up.
Notably, Chinese supply chains remain deeply embedded in Iveco's overseas business. The order for 100 minibuses in Azerbaijan that Iveco won in October this year will be assembled by Nanjing Iveco; its 2026 eDaily also adds a CATL lithium iron phosphate battery option.
For Chinese commercial vehicle makers such as Foton and Yutong that are stepping up investment in Europe and Latin America, Tata-owned Iveco will be a harder rival to avoid: the European brand's existing products, plants and service network could gain a more competitive cost structure thanks to Indian procurement and R&D capabilities. Chinese automakers' overseas expansion will increasingly face sustained competition from a single group.

articles.title: Malaysia’s Electronics Exports Ride the AI Boom - Electronics For You BUSINESS
articles.summary: Malaysia’s Electronics Exports Ride the AI Boom  Electronics For You BUSINESS
articles.full_text:
Malaysia’s exports rose 34% to RM1.571 trillion in the first nine months of 2026, as AI and semiconductor demand drove a RM253.88 billion increase in electrical and electronics export value.
Malaysia’s exports rose 34% to RM1.571 trillion in January–September 2026, with electrical and electronics shipments gaining RM253.88 billion as demand for AI hardware and semiconductors boosted trade.
Electrical and electronics (E&E) products, including semiconductors, printed circuit boards (PCBs) and passive components, were key contributors to Malaysia’s record nine-month export performance, according to the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE).
Growing demand for AI hardware and data-centre infrastructure supported electronics shipments, strengthening Malaysia’s role in the global semiconductor supply chain through chip assembly and testing operations.
Malaysia’s total trade reached RM2.91 trillion, up 30.1% year-on-year. Imports rose 25.7% to RM1.339 trillion, driven partly by intermediate goods such as semiconductor wafers, chemical feedstocks and machinery used by export-oriented industries. The country recorded a trade surplus of RM232.38 billion.
Exports to non-traditional markets, including Africa, Central Asia, South Asia and Latin America, increased 21.5% to RM136.36 billion, indicating broader market diversification. Exports to free trade agreement partners reached RM986.38 billion, accounting for 62.8% of total exports.
However, the outlook depends on sustained semiconductor demand and AI infrastructure investment. Normalising lead times, potential changes in hyperscaler spending, semiconductor export controls and competition from Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia could affect future growth.
MATRADE Director-General Indera Abu Bakar Yusof attributed the performance to the resilience of Malaysian exporters and small and medium-sized enterprises, alongside efforts to help domestic businesses enter emerging markets.

articles.title: Vietnam's cashew exports exceed US$4.2 billion in first 10 months - SGGP English Edition
articles.summary: Vietnam's cashew exports exceed US$4.2 billion in first 10 months  SGGP English Edition
articles.full_text:
Vietnam exported more than 600,000 tons of cashew kernels worth over US$4.2 billion through October 2026, with China and the United States accounting for the largest shares of imports at 21.6 percent and 15.2 percent, respectively, according to the Vietnam Cashew Association (VINACAS).
The figures were released at the 15th Vietnam International Cashew Conference (GCR 2026), jointly organized by VINACAS and the Ministry of Industry and Trade's Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency in Ho Chi Minh City on October 27.
Held under the theme “From Raw Materials to Added Value: Connecting Value Chains and Shaping the Future of Global Cashew Supply Chains,” the two-day event brought together more than 350 industry leaders, business representatives and experts from 40 countries and territories.
Part of Vietnam's national trade promotion program, the conference aimed to facilitate business networking and strengthen cooperation across the cashew industry.
Opening the event, VINACAS Chairman Pham Van Cong described the cashew sector as an interconnected global supply and value chain in which stakeholders' roles and interests are closely linked.
The industry continues to face challenges in 2026, including changes in tariff policies, rising trade barriers and fluctuations in production, transportation, logistics and financing costs. These pressures affect the entire supply chain, from raw material production and processing plants to commercial operations and end consumers, he said.
Mr. Pham Van Cong stressed that the industry must address immediate challenges while pursuing a more sustainable and resilient development path that generates greater value over the next 10 to 20 years.
During the conference, international speakers shared insights into crop seasons, consumption trends, markets for value-added cashew products, quality control, and food safety. Participants also discussed supply chain management, sustainability and emerging trends shaping the future of the global cashew industry.
VINACAS has set a target of exporting 800,000 tons of cashew kernels worth US$5 billion in 2026, underscoring the industry's ambition to expand exports and strengthen its position in international markets.

articles.title: made by Fressko Amazon Australia Sales Grow by 71% with Pattern - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: made by Fressko Amazon Australia Sales Grow by 71% with Pattern  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Buy-sell partnership helps sustainable drinkware brand improve availability, Buy Box performance and marketplace growth
MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Melbourne-based sustainable drinkware brand made by Fressko has grown sales on Amazon Australia by more than 71% in the past quarter through its partnership with global ecommerce and marketplace accelerator Pattern.
Founded in Melbourne in 2014 by childhood friends Sean Atme and Lucas Ciancarelli, made by Fressko has grown from a reusable coffee cup start-up into a global drinkware brand, with a range spanning coffee cups, water bottles, tumblers and accessories. As the business expanded, ecommerce increased its customer base, helping the brand to enter new markets and drive sales both in Australia and internationally.
While Amazon Australia became an increasingly important sales channel for made by Fressko, managing the growing complexity of the marketplace was becoming a challenge for its existing ecommerce team.
made by Fressko partnered with Pattern to grow its Amazon business, using a buy-sell model where Pattern purchases inventory directly from the brand and manages marketplace sales.
"As a growing brand with an expanding Australian and international presence, partnering with Pattern gives us the opportunity to accelerate our growth by leveraging their expertise, resources and capabilities," explained Damien Zumbo, International Sales Manager at made by Fressko.
"Working with Pattern has taken that pressure off our team and given us access to the technology, expertise and insights to grow the channel."
Since the partnership began, made by Fressko's Amazon in-stock rate has risen from 63% to 91%, contributing to its increased Buy Box win rate percentage, which has more than doubled (42% to 97%).
Pattern has optimised made by Fressko's Amazon advertising and content, using data and technology to direct advertising spend where it can drive additional sales, alongside improvements to product images, brandstore & A+ content, keywords and search engine optimisation. This has resulted in made by Fressko achieving an average return on advertising spend (ROAS) of around 8.2x, while advertising costs have remained relatively steady as sales have grown.
"Strong marketplace advertising isn't about spending more, it's about spending strategically," said Merline McGregor, Managing Director, at Pattern Australia.
"For made by Fressko, we've used Pattern's proprietary data and technology to identify where advertising can drive additional sales and where the brand is already performing well organically, continually adjusting investment accordingly. Achieving a strong return on investment while avoiding increases in advertising costs clearly demonstrates the impact of making a brand's spend work harder."

articles.title: India’s 2026–27 US$30.92 bil rail plan may boost Thai exports - Asia News Network
articles.summary: India’s 2026–27 US$30.92 bil rail plan may boost Thai exports  Asia News Network
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK – Thai machinery and cable exporters could benefit from India’s US$30.92 billion railway investment programme for 2026–27, according to a report published on 22 October 2026 by the Thai Trade Center in Mumbai. However, procurement restrictions and contracts already awarded limit access to the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed project.
Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai identified potential demand for specialised construction machinery, electrical machinery, wires and cables, safety equipment, industrial materials and technologies used in railway construction. Opportunities could extend to construction supply chains, systems installation and maintenance, depending on actual purchasing demand, contract terms and Indian technical and safety requirements.
India’s railway investment allocation amounts to approximately 2.93 trillion rupees and covers the wider network, not only the Mumbai–Ahmedabad line. As of April 2026, the country had approved 514 railway development projects covering approximately 40,000 kilometres.
Japanese loan conditions limit access to Mumbai–Ahmedabad contracts
Japanese government loans supporting the Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail project carry funding-linked procurement conditions, known as tied procurement, according to the Embassy of Japan in India. Those conditions mean progress on the railway does not automatically translate into purchasing opportunities for Thai suppliers.
Work on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad line’s signalling and train control systems, telecommunications and operations control centre has already been awarded to a consortium involving India’s Dineshchandra R. Agrawal Infracon and Germany’s Siemens.
Thai businesses considering India’s railway market need to examine individual contract status, rules of origin, technical specifications and supplier eligibility. Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai also highlighted competition from manufacturers in India, Japan and other countries, as well as import duties and freight costs that could weaken Thai products’ competitiveness.
Thai electrical exports to India provide an existing trade base
Thailand exported approximately US$1.43 billion worth of electrical machinery and equipment to India under Harmonised System (HS) Chapter 85 in 2025, up 7.9% from the previous year, according to trade figures cited by Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai.
Thai exports to India of insulated electrical wires and cables under HS code 8544 were worth approximately US$29.8 million in 2025, an increase of 13.3% year on year.
Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai sees the existing electrical and infrastructure-related export base as a foundation for further expansion in India. Businesses would still need to assess the requirements of individual railway contractors and buyers before pursuing supply opportunities.
Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed railway reaches 62.16% completion
The National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL), which is implementing India’s first high-speed railway, reported 62.16% overall physical progress on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad project, according to Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai.
Construction of all 14 portal beams supporting the elevated railway in Vadodara, Gujarat, has been completed. NHSRCL has also acquired the full 1,389.49 hectares required for the project and installed viaduct girders along more than 366 kilometres of the 508-kilometre route.
The Mumbai–Ahmedabad project includes a 21-kilometre tunnel section with a seven-kilometre undersea stretch. Tunnel boring machines are being used alongside the New Austrian Tunnelling Method, with 4.88 kilometres completed using the latter method.
Breakthroughs have also been achieved in four of the Mumbai–Ahmedabad project’s eight mountain tunnels, according to the progress figures cited by Thailand’s trade office in Mumbai.
Construction of the Mumbai–Ahmedabad railway’s Sabarmati maintenance depot is 32.28% complete, compared with 17.23% at the Thane depot. Track slabs have been installed along 97 kilometres of the route, with associated cement asphalt mortar injection work to fill gaps beneath the slabs.
Thailand’s Commerce Ministry ready to help rail exporters
Thailand’s Commerce Ministry is ready to support business matching between Thai suppliers and Indian contractors, alongside registration and certification with the Research Designs and Standards Organisation, India’s railway technical standards body.
The Thai trade office in Mumbai advised businesses to monitor NHSRCL and check which procurement contracts could accept new manufacturers or suppliers. Cooperation with Indian contractors and companies, supported by the necessary product standards and certification, would help Thai firms assess their prospects for entering railway supply chains.

articles.title: Efforts to join global supply chains - Nhan Dan Online
articles.summary: Efforts to join global supply chains  Nhan Dan Online
articles.full_text:
Building on success stories
As one of Viet Nam’s leading providers of technical services to the oil and gas and industrial sectors, PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC) — a subsidiary of the Viet Nam National Industry and Energy Group — recently completed, launched, and successfully transported four offshore substations for the Baltica 2 project off the coast of Poland. This marked the first time an offshore wind power product manufactured in Viet Nam had been exported to Europe. The achievement demonstrates Viet Nam’s engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contracting capabilities and represents a strategic step forward for the oil and gas sector in the global renewable energy supply chain.
With a strong focus on export-oriented manufacturing under models such as Free on Board (FOB), which involves sourcing materials, manufacturing, and selling finished goods, and Original Design Manufacturing (ODM), which includes product design and manufacturing, Garment 10 Corporation has gradually established itself as an important link in global supply chains, exporting products to more than 60 countries and territories. Alongside its established domestic labels, the company has recently developed several brands targeting export markets. These include DeTheia, a premium womenswear line, and Generos, a brand aimed at younger consumers. By making extensive use of social media platforms and e-commerce, the company has achieved impressive results, with Garment 10-branded products now sold in 19 countries, including demanding markets such as the US, the UK, and other European countries.
Over more than 30 years of economic opening and international integration, Viet Nam has gradually become an important link in global production and trade networks. Deeper participation in free trade agreements, the attraction of foreign direct investment (FDI), and the development of export-oriented manufacturing industries have helped expand trade rapidly. Between 2021 and 2025 alone, merchandise exports rose from 336.25 billion USD to 475.04 billion USD. However, this expansion has not been matched by a corresponding and sustained strengthening of domestic businesses’ role. In 2025, domestic enterprises accounted for just 22.7% of export turnover, while FDI enterprises accounted for 77.3%.
The gap is also evident in the extent of participation in global value chains and the ability to generate value. The proportion of domestic enterprises linked to global value chains fell from around 35% in 2009 to 18% in 2023. Services account for approximately 12% of total exports, while highly skilled workers make up only around 5% of the workforce in the processing and manufacturing sector. This shows that Viet Nam’s challenge is not simply to increase the number of domestic exporters but also to connect local businesses more effectively with global production networks and gradually shift towards activities with greater knowledge content and higher added value.
 The substantial presence of FDI enterprises creates opportunities for domestic businesses to access technology, management standards, and markets. However, their ability to become suppliers and participate more deeply in global production networks remains limited.
Dr Do Dieu Huong, 
Deputy Director of the Centre for Strategy and Policy, Viet Nam Institute of Economics and World Affairs
Addressing this issue, Dr Do Dieu Huong, Deputy Director of the Centre for Strategy and Policy at the Viet Nam Institute of Economics and World Affairs, said the substantial presence of FDI enterprises has offered domestic businesses opportunities to access technology, management standards, and markets, however, their ability to become suppliers and integrate more deeply into global production networks remains inadequate. The issue lies not only in the proportion of local procurement but, more importantly, in the quality of business linkages. Domestic enterprises need to improve their ability to control quality, refine processes, handle data, and coordinate technical activities, eventually progressing towards product design, testing, and joint development. The main bottleneck, therefore, is not simply a lack of connections with FDI enterprises but a shortage of stable, substantive supply relationships that foster learning, technology accumulation, and capability upgrading.
Meeting standards
In practice, getting products from domestic businesses into global supply chains remains challenging. Companies must meet increasingly stringent technical requirements imposed by customers and markets, while Vietnamese enterprises often face disadvantages in terms of capital, management capabilities, and technological expertise. According to a representative of AEON, one of Japan’s leading retail groups, more than 90% of the products displayed on its shelves come from Vietnamese suppliers. When expanding into new localities, AEON proactively engages and negotiates with regional suppliers to increase the proportion of locally sourced products across its retail network, thereby contributing directly to regional economic development.
In addition to procurement, AEON is stepping up cooperation with Vietnamese businesses to develop high-quality private-label products at reasonable prices. However, some enterprises have not invested sufficiently in brand identity, making it difficult for them to compete directly with major brands. Many small businesses also struggle to complete legal documentation and obtain quality certifications, particularly those relating to raw material traceability.
The AEON representative also noted that Vietnamese businesses face high logistics operating costs and limited capacity to deliver goods across wide geographical areas. In addition, they often struggle to manage and implement traceability procedures when sourcing raw materials from multiple suppliers or farming households.
To participate more deeply in global supply chains, Vietnamese enterprises must comply with international standards and sustainability requirements. Beyond ensuring product quality, they must adhere to global codes of conduct, including requirements relating to environmental protection, labour management, working hours, and waste discharge under the Code of Conduct (CoC), particularly when manufacturing goods under contract or producing private-label products for export. Businesses must also strengthen their ability to supply goods on a wider scale and establish nationwide or network-wide delivery and distribution capabilities to ensure product availability.

Beyond ensuring product quality, they must adhere to global codes of conduct, including requirements relating to environmental protection, labour management, working hours, and waste discharge under the Code of Conduct (CoC), particularly when manufacturing goods under contract or producing private-label products for export.
According to the AEON representative
Cha Ji Ho, Deputy General Director in charge of Samsung Vietnam’s Purchasing Centre, added that since 2015, Samsung Viet Nam had worked with the Ministry of Industry and Trade, local authorities, and relevant agencies to help Vietnamese enterprises improve shop-floor operations, increase productivity and product quality, train specialised personnel, and develop smart factory models.
Going forward, Samsung will continue to work alongside Vietnamese enterprises, shifting from providing support to jointly building capabilities and from developing individual companies to strengthening the competitiveness of the wider ecosystem. Its focus will be on foundational areas such as production management, core technologies, digital transformation, automation, and human resource development. These efforts will help businesses meet Samsung’s standards while also improving their competitiveness in international markets.
Samsung also shared its hope the Government of Viet Nam will continue identifying and introducing domestic enterprises with the capacity and potential to join global supply chains. It further emphasised the importance of developing mechanisms and policies to attract investment in technological equipment that meets international standards, alongside strengthening the training of highly skilled workers.
From a tax policy perspective, Le Thi Duyen Hai, Vice President and Secretary-General of the Viet Nam Tax Consultants’ Association, observed that Vietnamese exports remain concentrated in sectors that generally generate limited added value, such as garment manufacturing, seafood processing, agricultural products, and steel. Meanwhile, most electronic products and components are produced by FDI enterprises. Global supply chains are undergoing substantial restructuring, with production locations being diversified, dependence on individual markets reduced, resilience strengthened, and supply chains shortened.
 Tax policy needs to shift its focus from attracting investment into Viet Nam towards upgrading domestic enterprises’ capabilities so that they can become high-value links in global supply chains.

Vice President and Secretary-General of the Viet Nam Tax Consultants’ Association 
Viet Nam has an opportunity to attract additional projects, orders and production activities relocating to Southeast Asia. More than 30,000 foreign-invested enterprises currently operate in Viet Nam. Although they account for only 3% of all businesses, they contribute more than 30% of government revenue from production and business activities. However, Viet Nam risks becoming a low-value-added assembly base, while domestic enterprises have yet to participate in service supply chains for FDI companies to the extent expected. PAM states that the CDL holder would remain in the CMV while the CLP holder is driving, but not necessarily in the passenger seat of the vehicle. FMCSA is required by statute to publish a notice explaining each exemption request. This notice does not indicate what decision FMCSA will ultimately reach on the request. After reviewing the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted, FMCSA will grant or deny the exemption.

Abstract:
The STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program was authorized through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA), amended and reauthorized in 2000, 2005, 2013 and 2022. The STOP (Services, Training, Officers, and Prosecutors) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program provides funding to states and territories for use by state, local, and Indian Tribal governments, courts, and victim service providers. This program enhances the capacity of local communities to develop and strengthen effective law enforcement and prosecution strategies to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking and to develop and strengthen comprehensive, holistic victim services. The grant funds must be distributed by STOP state administrators to subgrantees according to a statutory formula.
This information collection is necessary for the Attorney General and STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program grantees and subgrantees to comply with federal statutory reporting requirements. The information will be used for reports to Congress on the use of appropriated funds in support of the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. There are two sets of respondents—the STOP state administrators who allocate the STOP
( printed page 67612)
funds and the subgrantees who may include law enforcement agencies, prosecutors' offices, courts, and victim services organizations.
Overview of This Information Collection
1.
Type of Information Collection:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
2.
Title of the Form/Collection:
Annual Progress Report for the STOP Formula Grants Program.
3.
Agency form number, if any, and the applicable component of the Department of Justice sponsoring the collection:
Form Number: 1122-0003. U.S. Department of Justice, Office on Violence Against Women.
4.
Affected public who will be asked or required to respond, as well as a brief abstract:
Affected Public- State, local and Tribal governments. The affected public includes the 56 STOP state administrators (from 50 states, the District of Columbia and five territories and commonwealths (Guam, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands)) and their subgrantees.
5.
An estimate of the total number of respondents and the amount of time estimated for an average respondent to respond:
It is estimated that it will take the 56 respondents (STOP administrators) approximately one hour to complete an annual progress report. It is estimated that it will take approximately one hour for roughly 1,960 subgrantees [1]
to complete the relevant portion of the annual progress report. The Annual Progress Report for the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program is divided into sections that pertain to the different types of activities that subgrantees may engage in and the different types of subgrantees that receive funds,

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is announcing
( printed page 67566)
the availability of the latest major release of the MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) model, MOVES6. MOVES6 is the latest version of the EPA's state-of-the-science modeling tool for estimating emissions from cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles based on the latest data and regulations. MOVES6 is available for use in State Implementation Plans (SIPs) and transportation conformity analyses. This notice starts a two-year grace period before MOVES6 will be required for use in transportation conformity determinations, both in new regional emissions analyses and in new hot-spot analyses.
DATES:
The EPA's announcement of the MOVES6 emissions model for SIPs and transportation conformity determinations in States other than California is effective October 27, 2026. This announcement starts a two-year transportation conformity grace period that ends on October 27, 2028. After this date, MOVES6 will be required for use as the latest EPA emissions model for new transportation conformity analyses other than California in both regional emissions analyses and in hot-spot analyses.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For technical model questions regarding the use of MOVES6, please email
moves@epa.gov. For questions about SIPs, contact Kaitlyn Leffert at
leffert.kaitlyn@epa.gov. For questions about transportation conformity, contact Aaron Letterly at
letterly.aaron@epa.gov.

MOVES6 is the EPA's latest official motor vehicle emissions model for State and local agencies to estimate volatile organic compounds (VOCs), nitrogen oxides (NOX), particulate matter (PM2.5

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 23, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam Zaleski, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA is 3,080 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026) and reallocations (91 FR 64807, October 13, 2026 and 91 FR 66531, October 21, 2026).
( printed page 67529)
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA will be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and 679.20(d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 2,480 mt and is setting aside 0 mt as incidental catch because it is not necessary to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA to prevent exceeding this sector's annual allocation of Pacific cod TAC.
While this closure is effective the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on Pacific cod catch in a timely fashion and would delay the closure of directed fishing for Pacific cod by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on Pacific cod catch by vessels using pot gear in the Western Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 22, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after the date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

                    SUMMARY:
In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) a request for review and approval of the information collection listed below.
                    DATES:
Comments regarding this information collection are best assured of having their full effect if received by November 27, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    This proposed information collection was previously published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     on August 6, 2026, page 50864 (Vol. 91, No. 450) and allowed 60 days for public comment. No comments were received. The purpose of this notice is to allow an additional 30 days for public comment. The Clinical Center, National Institutes of Health, may not conduct or sponsor, and the respondent is not required to respond to, an information collection that has been extended, revised, or implemented on or after October 1, 1995, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
                
In compliance with Section 3507(a)(1)(D) of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) a request for review and approval of the information collection listed below.
                    Proposed Collection Title:
                     Application Process for Clinical Research Training and Medical Education at the NIH Clinical Center and Its impact on Course and Training Program Enrollment and Effectiveness, 0925-0698, REVISION, Exp., date October 31, 2026, National Institutes of Health Clinical Center (CC), National Institutes of Health (NIH).
                
                    Need and Use of Information Collection:
                     The primary objective of the application process is to allow the Office of Clinical Research Training and Medical Education (OCRTME) at the NIH Clinical Center to evaluate applicants' qualifications to determine applicants' eligibility for training programs managed by the Office. Applicants must provide the required information requested in the respective applications to be considered a candidate for participation. Information submitted by candidates for training programs is reviewed initially by OCRTME administrative staff to establish eligibility for participation. Eligible candidates are then referred to the designated training program director/administrator or training program selection committee for review and decisions regarding acceptance for participation. Upon acceptance, OCRTME will collect required eligibility documents for respective training programs. A secondary objective of the application process is to track enrollment in training programs over time.
                
OMB approval is requested for 3 years. There are no costs to respondents other than their time. The total estimated annualized burden hours 400.

AGENCY:
National Science Foundation; National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics within the National Science Foundation (NSF) is announcing plans to request renewal of the Survey of Earned Doctorates (OMB Control Number 3145-0019) . In accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, we are providing opportunity for public comment on this action. After obtaining and considering public comments, NCSES will prepare the submission requesting OMB clearance of this collection for three years.
DATES:
Written comments on this notice must be received by December 28, 2026 to be assured consideration. Comments received after that date will be considered to the extent practicable. Send comments to the address below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Suzanne H. Plimpton, Reports Clearance Officer, U.S. National Science Foundation, Randolph Building, 401 Dulany Street, Alexandria, Virginia 22314; telephone (703) 292-7556; or send email to
splimpto@nsf.gov.
Individuals who use a telecommunications device for the deaf (TDD) may call the Federal Information Relay Service (FIRS) at 1-800-877-8339, which is accessible 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year (including Federal holidays).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title of Collection:
Survey of Earned Doctorates.
OMB Control Number:
3145-0019.
Expiration Date of Current Approval:
June 30, 2028.
Type of Request:
Intent to seek approval to renew information collection for three years.
Abstract:
Established within the NSF by the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 section 505, codified in the NSF Act of 1950, as amended, the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) serves as a central Federal clearinghouse for the collection, interpretation, analysis, and dissemination of objective data on science, engineering, technology, and research and development for use by practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and the public.
The Survey of Earned Doctorates (SED) is part of NCSES' portfolio and collects data on individuals to provide information on science and engineering education and careers in the United States. The SED has been conducted annually since 1958 and is jointly sponsored by four Federal agencies (NSF/NCSES, National Institutes of Health, U.S. Department of Education/National Center for Education Statistics, and National Endowment for the Humanities) to avoid duplication of effort in collecting such data. It is an accurate, timely source of information on our Nation's highly educated individuals. This request to renew the information collection for three years is to cover the 2028 and 2029 SED survey cycles.
Data are obtained via Web survey from each person earning a research doctorate from an accredited U.S. institution at the time they receive the degree. Data are collected on their field of specialty, educational background, sources of support in graduate school, debt level, postgraduation plans, and demographic characteristics. NCSES publishes statistics from the survey in several reports. The survey will be collected in conformance with the Privacy Act of 1974. Responses from individuals are voluntary. NCSES will ensure that all individually identifiable information collected will be kept strictly confidential and will be used only for research or statistical purposes.
Use of the Information:
The Federal Government, policy makers, universities, researchers, and others use the information extensively. Results from the SED are used to assess characteristics of the doctorate population and trends in doctoral education and degrees. Data from the survey are published annually on the NCSES website in a publication series reporting on all fields of study, titled
Doctorate Recipients from U.S. Universities
(
https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf26315). Information from the SED is also included in other series available online such as
Science and Engineering Indicators (https://ncses.nsf.gov/indicators).
In addition, access to tabular data from selected variables is available through the NCSES online data tool (
https://ncsesdata.nsf.gov/builder/sed) and the SED Restricted Data Analysis System (
https://ncsesdata.nsf.gov/rdas/#/).
Expected Respondents:
The SED is a census of all individuals receiving a research doctorate from an accredited U.S. academic institution in the academic year beginning July 1 and ending June 30 of the subsequent year. As such, the population for the 2028 SED consists of all individuals receiving a research doctorate in the 12-month period beginning July 1, 2027 and ending June 30, 2028. Likewise, the population for the 2029 SED consists of all individuals receiving a research doctorate in the 12-month period beginning July 1, 2028 and ending June 30, 2029. A research doctorate is a doctoral degree that (1) requires completion of an original intellectual contribution in the form of a dissertation or an equivalent culminating project (
e.g.,
musical composition) and (2) is not primarily intended as a degree for the practice of a profession. The most common research doctorate degree is the Ph.D. Recipients of professional doctoral degrees, such as MD, DDS, JD, DPharm, and PsyD, are not included in the SED. The 2028 and 2029 SED are expected to include about 615 separately reporting schools with eligible research doctoral programs from about 480 doctorate-granting institutions. Based on the historical trend, NCSES expects a stable turnout of research doctorates for the next few years with a nominal increase from the 2026 cycle estimating that approximately 62,000 individuals will receive a research doctorate from U.S. institutions in each of the 2028 cycle and the 2029 cycle.
In addition to the questionnaire for individuals receiving their research doctorates, the SED needs to collect administrative data such as graduation lists from participating academic institutions. An Institutional Coordinator at each institution helps distribute the Web survey link, track
( printed page 67615)
survey completions, and submit information to the SED survey contractor.
Estimate of Burden:
An average overall response rate of 91.5% of the persons who earned a research doctorate from a U.S. institution was obtained in the academic years 2023, 2024, and 2025. Using the past response rate, the number of SED respondents in each cycle is estimated to be 56,730 (62,000 doctorate recipients × 0.915 response rate) in each of the 2028 and 2029 cycles.
