articles.title: Critical Material List; Addition of Helium
articles.summary: The United States (U.S.) Department of Energy (DOE) is issuing this notice to advise the public that DOE added helium to the DOE Critical Material List. This notice also provides the link to the assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List. Helium is non-substitutable for multiple critical energy functions, including: semiconductor manufacturing, leak testing natural gas infrastructure, and quantum computing, along with being essential to key medical...
articles.full_text:
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Section 7002(a)(2) of the Energy Act of 2020 (Pub. L. 116-260, div. Z, 134 Stat. 2418) defines “critical materials” to be: any non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the Secretary of Energy determines has high risk for supply chain disruption and serves an essential function in one or more energy technologies, including technologies that produce, transmit, store, and conserve energy (referred to here as a critical material for energy) or a critical mineral (as designated by the Secretary of the Interior).[] 
                    
                
                    On August 4, 2023, DOE published its Notice of Final Determination on 2023 DOE Critical Materials List (“Critical Materials List”).[] 
                    
                     The Critical Materials List includes the following:
                
                    Critical materials for energy:
                     aluminum, cobalt, copper*, dysprosium, electrical steel* (grain-oriented electrical steel, non-grain-oriented electrical steel, and amorphous steel), fluorine, gallium, iridium, lithium, magnesium, natural graphite, neodymium, nickel, platinum, praseodymium, terbium, silicon*, and silicon carbide*.[] 
                    
                
                    Critical minerals:
                     The Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), published a 2022 final list of critical minerals that includes the following 50 minerals: Aluminum, antimony, arsenic, barite, beryllium, bismuth, cerium, cesium, chromium, cobalt, dysprosium, erbium, europium, fluorspar, gadolinium, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, holmium, indium, iridium, lanthanum, lithium, lutetium, magnesium, manganese, neodymium, nickel, niobium, palladium, platinum, praseodymium, rhodium, rubidium, ruthenium, samarium, scandium, tantalum, tellurium, terbium, thulium, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium, ytterbium, yttrium, zinc, and zirconium.
                
                    The critical materials for energy included on the Critical Material List are based on the criticality assessed in the short- and medium-term. A detailed description of DOE's methodology can be found in its Critical Minerals Assessment published on its website in July 2023.[] 
                    
                     On May 22, 2025, metallurgical grade coal for steelmaking was added to DOE's list of critical materials for energy.[] 
                    
                
                    By this notice, the Secretary of Energy advises the public of the addition of helium to DOE's Critical Material List. The assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List can be found on DOE's website: 
                    https://www.energy.gov/cmm/what-are-critical-materials-and-critical-minerals.
                     The assessment concludes that helium is needed globally for semiconductor manufacturing and other key energy applications. Meeting the policy goal of building U.S. SI infrastructure will require expansion of semiconductor production and thereby supports the determination that helium is a DOE critical material.
                
                    Furthermore, this action directly supports the President's policy goal of “Winning the AI Race: America's AI Action Plan” [] 
                    
                     and “Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure”.[] 
                    
                
Signing Authority
                    This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 21, 2026, by Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary, Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the 
                    Federal Register
                    .
                
                    Signed in Washington, DC, on October 23, 2026.
Jennifer Hartzell,
Alternate Federal Register Liaison Officer, U.S. Department of Energy.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, DHS.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Coast Guard announces that it is adding the Federal Republic of Somalia to the Port Security Advisory.
DATES:
The policy announced in this notice is effective on October 27, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about this document call or email Mr. Edward Munoz, Division Chief, International Port Security Assessments, U.S. Coast Guard, telephone 202-372-2122,
HQS-DG-IPSProgramHQs@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Purpose
The authority for this notice is 5 U.S.C. 552(a) (“Administrative Procedure Act”), 46 U.S.C. 70110 (“Maritime Transportation Security Act”), and Department of Homeland Security Delegation No. 0170.1(II)(97)(f). As delegated, section 70110(a) authorizes the U.S. Coast Guard to impose conditions of entry on vessels arriving in U.S. waters from ports that the U.S. Coast Guard has not found to maintain effective antiterrorism measures. Accordingly, the U.S. Coast Guard has determined that Somalia is not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures in its ports and is imposing conditions of entry on vessels arriving to the U.S. from the ports of Somalia.
With this notice, the current list of countries assessed and not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures is as follows: Cambodia, Cameroon, Comoros, Cuba, Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), Equatorial Guinea, Gambia (The), Guinea-Bissau, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Madagascar, Micronesia (Federated States of), Nauru, Sao Tome and Principe, Seychelles, Somalia, Sudan, Suriname, Syria, Timor-Leste, Venezuela, and Yemen. The current Port Security Advisory is available at:
http://www.dco.uscg.mil/Our-Organization/Assistant-Commandant-for-Prevention-Policy-CG-5P/International-Domestic-Port-Assessment/.
Nathan A. Moore,
Vice Admiral, USCG, Deputy Commandant for Operations.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Information Collection Request Title:
Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network Board of Directors and Committee Member Applications and Forms, OMB No. 0906-New.
Abstract:
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) is a public-private partnership that links professionals involved in the U.S. donation, procurement, and transplantation system. The OPTN focuses on promoting long, healthy, and productive lives for people with organ failure. The OPTN also aims to increase opportunities for transplants, optimize organ use, enhance efficiency, and prioritize patient care. The OPTN Board of Directors (BOD) is authorized by section 372 of the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984 (NOTA) (
see42 U.S.C. 274(b)(1)(B)), and the operation composition of the OPTN BOD are further codified in federal regulation under the regulations implementing NOTA (
see42 CFR 121.3(a)). These regulations also provide that the OPTN BOD shall “establish committees as are necessary to perform the duties of the OPTN” and describe the composition of these committees (see 42 CFR 121.3(a)(4)). As part of the ongoing OPTN Modernization Initiative (
https://www.hrsa.gov/optn-modernization/learn-more-about-modernization), HRSA seeks OMB approval of applications to be completed by candidates interested in volunteering to serve on the OPTN BOD and/or on the committees that support the BOD. Members of the OPTN BOD and committees do not receive payment for this work. HRSA also seeks approval of conflict-of-interest (COI), code of conduct, confidentiality, and attestation forms to be completed by the selected/confirmed members of the OPTN BOD, committees, and review boards on an annual, tri-annual, or ad hoc basis. The OPTN BOD consists of 35 members who serve 2 to 3-year terms and are supported by 21 committees with a total of approximately 419 members with the same term limits. Select members of the BOD also serve on committee(s) as Visiting Board Members. In addition, there are ad hoc committees or BOD workgroups that may be established to work on time-limited issues, and these members (approximately 20 a year) would fill out the annual COI form as well. Given some committee turnover, there are approximately 505 committee and BOD members filling out the annual COI form, code of conduct form, confidentiality form, and attestation form every year. In addition, approximately 841 members of OPTN Review Boards will fill out the annual COI form, confidentiality agreements, and code of conduct forms.

Federal Register
on August 6, 2026, Vol. 91, No. 150, FR pp. 50861. HRSA received comments from one entity, the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations. The commenter recognized the important role of volunteers within the OPTN and provided recommendations intended to clarify and improve the proposed Board of Directors and Committee Volunteer Interest Forms and the COI disclosure forms. The commenter recommended revisions to the forms related to questions concerning applicant disciplinary history, Organ Procurement Organization (OPO) roles and transplant programs, living and deceased donor experience, social media information, prior OPTN volunteer service, financial interests, and the frequency of recurring COI disclosures.
On Form 1, the commenter asked for the justification for requesting social media handles and expressed concern that they would be used to screen out applicants with divergent views.
HRSA Response:
HRSA removed an optional open-ended question regarding social media handles.
On Form 1, the commenter expressed concern that a question asking about an applicant's employer facing regulatory discipline could require an applicant to disclose confidential information.
HRSA Response:
HRSA revised the question concerning criminal, ethics, or regulatory disciplinary matters. The revised question no longer requests information concerning disciplinary matters involving an applicant's employer and separates the remaining inquiry into two yes/no questions addressing prior actions and currently pending matters regarding the applicant and not the employer.
On Form 1, the commenter also asked, for clarification purposes, to list “organ donor” as “living donor” and allowing for OPO experience to be marked as OPO-administrative versus OPO-clinical.
HRSA Response:
HRSA revised Form 1 and accepted both changes.
On Form 1, the commenter expressed concern that questions asking patient and family members about their advocacy and outreach experience may discourage people from applying if they lack this experience.
HRSA Response:
Regarding the comment that the questions may discourage applicants who lack outreach or advocacy experience, the form also asks for other background experience in areas such as finance, governance, and ethics. On Forms 1 and 2, the commenter suggested some questions did not appear to apply to the procurement side because they only mentioned transplantation experience.

articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
                    SUMMARY:
This document provides notice to customs brokers that the annual user fee that is assessed for each permit held by a customs broker, whether an individual, partnership, association, or corporation, is due no later than January 29, 2027. Pursuant to fee adjustments required by the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act) and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations, the customs broker permit user fee payable for calendar year 2027 will be $190.88.
                    DATES:
Payment of the 2027 Customs Broker Permit User Fee is due no later than January 29, 2027.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
                    Pursuant to section 111.96 of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) (19 CFR 111.96(c)), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) assesses an annual user fee for each customs broker permit granted to an individual, partnership, association, or corporation. The CBP regulations provide that this fee is payable each calendar year for a national permit held by a customs broker and must be paid by the due date published annually in the 
                    Federal Register
                    . See19 CFR 24.22(h) and (i); 19 CFR 111.96(c).
                
Section 24.22 of title 19 of the CFR (19 CFR 24.22) sets forth the terms and conditions for when fees for certain services, including specific customs user fees, are required. The specific customs user fee amounts that appear in 19 CFR 24.22 are not the actual fees but represent the base year amounts that are subject to adjustment each fiscal year in accordance with the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act) (Pub. L. 114-94, December 4, 2015). Section 32201 of the FAST Act amended section 13031 of the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) of 1985 (19 U.S.C. 58c) by requiring the Secretary of the Treasury to adjust certain customs COBRA user fees and corresponding limitations to reflect certain increases in inflation. Paragraph (k) of section 24.22 of title 19 of the CFR (19 CFR 24.22(k)) sets forth the methodology to adjust fees for inflation and to determine the change in inflation, including the factor by which the fees and limitations will be adjusted, if necessary.
                    Customs brokers are subject to an annual customs broker permit user fee calculated using the base year amount in Appendix A to 19 CFR part 24, as adjusted by the terms in 19 CFR 24.22(k). 
                    See19 U.S.C. 58c(a)(7) and 19 CFR 24.22(h). In accordance with 19 CFR 24.22, CBP determines annually whether an adjustment to the fees and limitations is necessary and publishes a 
                    Federal Register
                     notice specifying the amount of the fees and limitations for each fiscal year. On July 31, 2026, CBP published a 
                    Federal Register
                     notice, entitled Customs User Fees To Be Adjusted for Inflation in Fiscal Year 2027 (CBP Decision 26-14), which announced, among other fee adjustments, that the annual customs broker permit user fee will increase to $190.88 for calendar year 2027. 
                    See91 FR 48398.
                
                    Thus, as required by 19 CFR 24.22, CBP provided notice in the 
                    Federal Register
                     of the annual fee amount at least 60 days prior to the date that the payment is due for each customs broker national permit. This document notifies customs brokers that, for calendar year 2027, the due date for payment of the annual customs broker permit user fee is January 29, 2027. If a customs broker fails to pay the annual customs broker permit user fee by January 29, 2027, the national permit is revoked by operation of law. 
                    See19 CFR 111.45(b) and 111.96(c).
                
                    Customs brokers are strongly encouraged to submit the payment electronically via the eCBP portal located at 
                    https://e.cbp.dhs.gov/brokers/#/home.
                     Customs brokers who are first-time users of the eCBP portal must create a 
                    Login.gov
                     account. Instructions and training resources—such as user and quick reference guides for customs brokers on how to create a 
                    Login.gov
                     account and how to use the eCBP portal—can be found on CBP's website at 
                    https://www.cbp.gov/trade/eCBP.
                     CBP will also accept payments at the processing center as defined in 19 CFR 111.1, in accordance with the remittance procedures in 19 CFR 24.22(i).
                
                    Susan S. Thomas,
Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade.

AGENCY:
Federal Communications Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Enforcement Bureau (the “Bureau”) gives notice of the suspension of Richard Bernstein from the schools and libraries universal service support mechanism (or “E-Rate Program”) and all universal service support mechanisms. Additionally, the Bureau gives notice that debarment proceedings are commencing against Mr. Bernstein, or any person who has an existing contract with or intends to
( printed page 67573)
contract with him to provide or receive services in matters arising out of activities associated with or related to the schools and libraries support, may respond by filing an opposition request, supported by documentation.
DATES:
Opposition requests must be submitted within 30 days of receiving the suspension letter or by November 27, 2026, whichever comes first. The Bureau will decide on any opposition request within 90 days.
ADDRESSES:
Federal Communications Commission, Enforcement Bureau, Investigations and Hearings Division, 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC 20554.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jeffrey Brown, Federal Communications Commission, Enforcement Bureau, Investigations and Hearings Division, 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC 20554. Jeffrey Brown may be contacted by phone at (202) 418-2527 or by email at
Jeffrey.Brown@fcc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Bureau has suspension and debarment authority pursuant to 47 CFR 54.8 and 47 CFR 0.111(a)(14). Suspensions ensure that suspended parties cannot continue to benefit from the schools and libraries mechanism pending resolution of the debarment process. Attached is the suspension letter, DA 26-1123, which was mailed to Mr. Bernstein, and released on October 27, 2026. The complete text of the notice of suspension and initiation of debarment proceedings is available on the FCC's website at
https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-1123A1.pdf.
Federal Communications Commission.
Christopher Sova,
Chief, Investigations and Hearings Division, Enforcement Bureau.

articles.title: How Alex Lee became the first engineer at Magic Patterns
articles.summary: Alex Lee left his own startup to join Magic Patterns as founding engineer — and built a slide deck feature in a weekend.
articles.full_text:
Before Alex Lee joined Magic Patterns (W23), he was running his own company, Iago — one that's still self-running today.
But when his former Robinhood colleague Teddy co-founded Magic Patterns, a tool that helps product designers create interactive mockups and prototypes, Alex saw something he couldn't pass up: an AI-first approach to a problem he'd hit himself while building new features at Iago.
"It's pretty clear that Figma is going to be replaced and a company like Magic Patterns is here to replace it," he says.
Technically, Alex was employee number two — a sales hire came first — but he was already working part-time before he officially started.
Why Magic PatternsAlex already knew co-founder Teddy from Robinhood.
They'd stayed in touch, texting about startups and sharing philosophies about work and engineering.
"I felt like I aligned really well with Teddy and Alex" — the co-founders — "and how they thought, and felt like I'd not only grow but grow with the company if I joined.
"The problem space pulled him in, too.
Magic Patterns is used by more than 3,000 product teams, and Alex gets a front-row seat to how those teams are reshaping design in an AI world.
"Especially as the different product team roles — eng, design, product — start to blend, it's super interesting to see how fast everything's evolved, and stay on top of it.
"Owning problems, not just features"You're not just a code monkey, but you're also a product person," Alex says.
"Things move so fast at a small company that you don't just own features, you own problems.
And when you find solutions, you're in charge of finding the next set of problems to solve.
"That means coding, yes — but also improving the onboarding funnel, talking to customers, and jumping on support.
One weekend, Alex noticed users weren't just making designs but building slide decks to present those designs to leadership.
So he built out an entirely new file type with full slide deck features over the weekend and shipped it.
"A big company wouldn't even let me ship this without talking to the right team who 'owned' this product surface.
"He also landed on the front page of Hacker News with a side project done at work: an agent that builds Rollercoaster Tycoon-influenced theme parks from a prompt.
The daily toolkitAlex dogfoods Magic Patterns itself to design new features.
Once something is ready to implement, his workflow looks like this:Cursor and Claude Code, always on the latest modelsCursor connected to Slack — he prompts it directly for small bug fixes and featuresAn internal code reviewer agent called Patterson that reviews code before it shipsThree clones of the same GitHub repo instead of worktrees, so he can work on features in parallelTransparency as a featureAlex says the thing that surprised him most about startup life is how transparent it is.
"Everyone at Magic Patterns knows the financials, growth rate because the founders trust us, but also because they are building a very open and transparent culture.
" He actually thinks large companies carry more hidden risk.
"You never know when they might lay people off or have a change in direction.
"The founders, Teddy and Alex, foster a culture of trust and autonomy.
"They're incredibly receptive to feedback and will always take action on it.
"Now that the team has grown to ten people, Alex has taken on more interviewing and has become the dedicated forward-deployed engineer for enterprise customers, especially around Magic Patterns' Design Systems vertical — the top-requested enterprise feature.
Who should join"If you're early in your career, make a polarized bet," Alex says.
"You'll work more than a typical 9-5 but you'll be learning a lot more in return.
" If you want real ownership, the chance to ship a feature over a weekend, and a view overlooking Coit Tower from a new San Francisco office, Magic Patterns is hiring an engineer who wants to build the world's best AI design agents.

articles.full_text:
From the Archive–these posts are written by ChatGPT
These selections emphasize the quality of the criticism: original interpretations, close attention to the work, and arguments worth considering even when you disagree. They are not a ranking of the films and television shows themselves. The list includes five reviews by Tyler Cowen and six by Alex Tabarrok. Several of the original posts reveal major plot developments; the descriptions here keep those revelations to a minimum.
1. Tyler Cowen — The Devil Wears Prada: A Straussian Interpretation
July 2, 2006 · Film · Spoilers in the original review
“Make no mistake about it, this is a movie about sheer power lust.”
Cowen reads beneath the film’s apparent moral lesson about rejecting a demanding career. His interpretation asks which relationships the ending restores, whose approval still matters, and whether the heroine has actually escaped the ambitions she appears to renounce. The result is a compact argument about power, independence, and emulation. Why it belongs: A memorable example of Cowen’s ability to turn a popular entertainment into an argument about motives. Read it after watching, when you can assess his interpretation against the ending. Read Cowen’s original review
2. Alex Tabarrok — Fleabag and Killing Eve
June 6, 2019 · Television · Major spoilers
“Fleabag is much darker and more religious and mystical than most people realize.”
Tabarrok connects the two series through sexual power, moral agency, and religious failure. His reading of Fleabag draws on textual and visual parallels to argue that its comedy conceals a much darker moral structure. The comparison with Killing Eve expands the argument beyond a single protagonist. Why it belongs: One of his most ambitious pieces of television criticism. Its characterization is contestable, but the sustained interpretation gives readers something substantial to argue with. Read Tabarrok’s original review
3. Tyler Cowen — Toni Erdmann, Misunderstood Masterpiece
February 5, 2017 · Film · Major spoilers
“The emotionally unrewarding nature of contemporary cosmopolitan life, but also the limits of rootedness.”
Cowen brings together family relationships, corporate humiliation, gender, and the relationship between Germany and Eastern Europe. He resists treating the film as a simple celebration of authenticity against professional life. Both the cosmopolitan daughter and the father who disrupts her world become objects of scrutiny. Why it belongs: The review connects intimate discomfort to larger social structures without reducing the film to a single message. Cowen’s suggestion that some of the father’s appearances might be imaginary should be read as his speculative interpretation. Read Cowen’s original review
4. Alex Tabarrok — Perfect Days, in “What to Watch (or Not)”
August 7, 2025 · Film · Some spoilers
“the routine is also a narcotic for the lost.”
Tabarrok challenges the comforting interpretation of Perfect Days as a lesson in finding happiness through simple routines. He recognizes the beauty of the protagonist’s life while asking whether its carefully maintained rhythms also protect him from painful relationships. His discussion of “crown shyness” turns a natural image into a metaphor for emotional distance. Why it belongs: A concise, sensitive counterreading that allows beauty and avoidance to coexist. The film discussion appears within a composite post that also covers Ballard and Billy Joel. Read Tabarrok’s original review
5. Tyler Cowen — Her
December 29, 2013 · Film · Light spoilers
“Will they enslave us, will they be our dogs, our friends, our trading partners, or something else altogether?”
Cowen treats the film as an exploration of the possible relationships between humans and artificial intelligence. He also attends to its visual and literary ancestry, making the review more than a response to the premise. The central question is how unfamiliar forms of intelligence might fit into emotional and social life. Why it belongs: It captures intellectual excitement about a film while opening questions that extend far beyond it. Its 2013 date makes the discussion especially interesting to revisit amid later debates about AI companionship. Read Cowen’s original review
6. Alex Tabarrok — Contagion
September 19, 2011 · Film · Limited plot discussion
“we have been lucky not virtuous.”
Tabarrok uses the film to examine preparedness and the difficulty of taking rare but consequential risks seriously. The review’s force comes from the relationship between cinematic imagination and public attention: a movie can make a danger emotionally intelligible when abstract warnings fail. Why it belongs: A strong example of film criticism becoming an argument about institutions and risk perception. Read its scientific and preparedness claims in their historical context: this is a review written in 2011. Read Tabarrok’s original review
7. Tyler Cowen — Technology in Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey
June 17, 2018 · Film · Spoilers near the end
“Finally the Solow residual is explained!”
Cowen combines observations about technological forecasting with attention to cinematic form, musical pacing, and narrative risk. The economic joke is characteristic, but the review also makes a case for the film’s sensory power and for seeing it on a large screen. Why it belongs: An entertaining blend of economic thinking and aesthetic attention. It shows how a familiar classic can yield fresh observations when approached through several disciplines at once. Read Cowen’s original review
8. Alex Tabarrok — Daredevil and the Doctrine of Double Effect
November 25, 2018 · Television · Some season-three details
“As I thought about this more, however, the Thou Shall Not Kill trope is least objectionable in Daredevil.”
Tabarrok starts with an objection to the superhero convention against killing, then revises his judgment by considering Daredevil’s Catholic commitments. The interesting move is to assess the character’s choices within his own moral framework rather than only through the viewer’s preferred calculation of consequences. Why it belongs: Criticism that visibly changes its mind. The post offers a useful discussion of character consistency and moral reasoning; its account of theology is best treated as part of that argument rather than a comprehensive doctrinal explanation. Read Tabarrok’s original review
9. Tyler Cowen — Borgen Season Four
July 23, 2022 · Television · Thematic spoilers
“I wish the content had more of ‘my kind of liberalism,’ but maybe the right-wing cultural critique makes for better TV.”
Cowen considers political power, gender, Greenland, and the media while separating his political preferences from his judgment of the drama. He asks whether a critique he finds less congenial might nevertheless produce stronger television. Why it belongs: A particularly clear example of judging artistic achievement independently of ideological agreement. The post is most revealing as a reflection on what makes political drama work. Read Cowen’s original review
10. Alex Tabarrok — The Remarkable Life of Ibelin
January 16, 2025 · Documentary · Reveals the film’s central turn
“What defines an ideal romance? What constitutes true friendship?”
Tabarrok explores how the documentary changes our understanding of a disabled young man’s life through his online relationships. Its construction prompts questions about intimacy, embodiment, and the limits of what even close relatives can know about another person. Why it belongs: A humane review that uses the documentary’s form to reconsider the value of online life. Although the original post labels itself “No spoilers,” readers who want to experience the central revelation unprepared should watch first. Read Tabarrok’s original review
11. Alex Tabarrok — The Gaslighting of Parasite
June 25, 2020 · Film · Major spoilers
“the most willfully misinterpreted movie that I have ever seen.”
Tabarrok challenges the prevailing interpretation of Parasite as an indictment of economic inequality. He builds his counterreading around the families’ conduct, the poorer characters’ treatment of other workers, and recurring imagery of smell and contamination. He argues that the film’s moral judgments cut against the political expectations many critics bring to it. Why it belongs: One of his most provocative and sustained film interpretations, and an essential inclusion in this selection. His reading is contestable, especially his insistence that the film’s judgments are unambiguous. That tension makes it rewarding to discuss alongside Cowen’s The Devil Wears Prada review: both ask whether a film’s apparent message conceals a different account of power and ambition. Read Tabarrok’s original review

Emily Bazelon was the moderator, there were five of us in the symposium.  Excerpt from me:

Bores: Do you think the federal government pre-empting the states is consistent with democracy?
Cowen: Absolutely. We have federal laws that pre-empt state lawmaking in many other areas. Courts have upheld it many, many times.
Bores: OK, but is it pro-democracy, in giving people a say?
Cowen: It is pro-American Constitution.

Most of the panel disagreed with most of my points.

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boomTrillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major compa...
articles.full_text:
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

articles.title: Is “Who’s on First?” funny?
articles.summary:
Well, no, it is not funny, it would be too easy to relieve the dramatic tension by having Abbott explain the actual situation to Costello.  One is not wrong to call the whole thing stupid. Yet there is another reading of the skit which stands at least some chance of being funny, though it is […]
The post Is “Who’s on First?” funny? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Well, no, it is not funny, it would be too easy to relieve the dramatic tension by having Abbott explain the actual situation to Costello.  One is not wrong to call the whole thing stupid.

Yet there is another reading of the skit which stands at least some chance of being funny, though it is not funny either.
You will note that Louis Costello was an Italian-American and son of an immigrant, and he had the obvious class mannerisms of such a stereotype.  Bud Abbott was half Jewish and I believe half some mainstream ethnicity.  He is a stand-in for the establishment, part of which was Jewish and highly commercial.  You can read the skit as a commentary on how the establishment rips off the “less tutored” immigrants and refuses to apologize for that or even to explain it.  The establishment simply keeps on talking rings around the lower-class immigrant, whether or not those words make sense.  The immigrant has no real recourse, as he is less articulate and is also less in control and can only play the role of boob.  In essence, Abbott, by not telling Costello the real names of the players, is not letting the ethnic assimilate into that most American of pasttimes, namely baseball.
Note how Costello admits, early in the skit, that he is the one with the funny name (Sebastian Dinwitty in the skit, likely a take-off on “dimwit”).  And Abbott, by speaking of the players as being named Who, What, and “I don’t know,” is expressing his frustration with an America that does not sound or look the same any more.  Abbott is in essence saying “Hey, what is this?  I was not expecting Ted Kluszewski in my country!”  He is throwing the growing presence of immigrants in the country back in the face of the ethnic and then stonewalling it.
In the skit, Abbott has the name of “Mr. Broadhurst,” very reminiscent of the establishment.
The skit does show we had an America too obsessed with names, and to no fruitful purpose.  It is no accident that in addition to the “hames” for all the baseball players, we are given names for the skit characters as well, even though that might appear not necessary for the unfolding of the dialogue as it usually is understood.
Racist is not the right word, but the skit plays on ethnic prejudices in a manner which one can rightfully find somewhat uncomfortable.  The back and forth dynamic reflects the prejudices of American life, though the presenters mirror and amplify those dynamics rather than merely critiquing them.  And (again) while the skit is not funny, this interpretation at least opens a door to some people finding it funny.
When Larry David and Seinfeld note they were influenced by Abbott and Costello, they (especially LD) sometimes deploy ethnic stereotypes in a similar manner.
Of course I, being from northern New Jersey, would happen upon this interpretation of Abbott and Costello.
By the way, Costello grew up in Paterson, New Jersey.  Abbott was born in Asbury Park, New Jersey, and he grew up in Coney Island.  I wonder if they thought the skit was funny.
Elizabeth Holmes, in the recent You Can See Everything Movie, was right to say she did not understand the skit.  She grew up in WDC until age nine and then Houston, plus she was born too late.  Furthermore, she is used to a world where you hire a guy named “Hu,” right?

AGENCY:
National Institutes of Health, HHS.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The invention listed below is owned by an agency of the U.S. Government and is available for licensing to achieve expeditious commercialization of results of federally-funded research and development. Foreign patent applications are filed on selected inventions to extend market coverage for companies and may also be available for licensing.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Inquiries related to this licensing opportunity should be directed to: Jonathan Motley at 240-669-5209, or
jonathan.motley@nih.gov.
Licensing information may be obtained by communicating with the Technology Transfer and Intellectual Property Office, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, 5601 Fishers Lane, Rockville, MD 20852; tel. 301-496-2644. A signed Confidential Disclosure Agreement will be required to receive copies of unpublished information related to the invention.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Technology description follows:
Compositions and Methods for Detecting Lymphatic Filariasis
Description of Technology
Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis; LF) is a neglected tropical disease characterized by painful deformation of the host. LF affects over 120 million people throughout the tropics and subtropics of Asia, Africa, the Western Pacific, and parts of the Caribbean and South America. LF results from infection with the filarial parasites
Wuchereria bancrofti
or
Brugia malayi.
Current methods of confirming active
( printed page 67594)
infection by
W. bancrofti
or
B. malayi
include microscopy and immunoassays using serum/plasma extracted from the patient. However, the sensitivity of microscopy detection varies among patients, and existing immunoassays show cross-reactivity with antibodies directed towards other parasites, such as
Onchocerca volvulus
or
Loa loa,
whose geographic distribution can overlap with the LF-causing filarial parasites.
This new technology addresses the limitation of cross-reactivity, presenting an opportunity for a directed assay towards the detection of
W. bancrofti
or
B. malayi.
Preliminary data against sera from LF-affected individuals indicates Wb4 is effective at detecting
B. malayi.
Wb4B, a modified version of recombinant Wb4 that lacks the nineteen (19) amino acid signal sequence of full-length Wb4, appears capable of isolation and purification by traditional molecular biology techniques and shows improved response in immunoassays.
The subject technology, including the antigen sequence for Wb4B and plasmids enabling bacterial, insect, and mammalian cell expression, is available for licensing for commercial development in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 209 and 37 CFR part 404, as well as for further development and evaluation under a research collaboration.
There may be the potential to combine this technology with other NIAID-developed biomarker technologies (Wb123, available for licensing, HHS Ref. No. E-281-2010-0, “Diagnostic Assays and Methods of Use for Detection of Filarial Infection” and Wb5, available for licensing, HHS Ref. No. E-093-2022-0, “Compositions and Methods for Detecting Lymphatic Filariasis”) for the development of a multiplex assay for detection of active
W. bancrofti
or
B. malayi
infection for diagnostic or surveillance purposes.
Potential Commercial Applications:
Diagnostics forW. bancrofti
and
B. malayi
infection.
Surveillance forW. bancrofti
and
B. malayi
prevalence.
Competitive Advantages:
Increased specificity compared to available diagnostics.
Differentiation from other parasites with similar geographic footprints.
Development Stage:
Pre-Clinical.
Inventors:
Dr. Thomas B. Nutman and Dr. Sasisekhar Bennuru, both of NIAID.
Intellectual Property:
HHS Reference No. E-067-2024-0. U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 63/672,667, filed on July 17, 2024, and PCT Application No. PCT/US2025/037585, filed on July 17, 2025.
Related Inventions:
Diagnostic Assays and Methods of Use for Detection of Filarial Infection (HHS Reference No. E-281-2010-0); Compositions and Methods for Detecting Lymphatic Filariasis (HHS Reference No. E-093-2022-0).
Licensing Contact:
To license this technology, please contact Jonathan Motley at 240-669-5209, or
jonathan.motley@nih.gov,
and reference E-067-2024-0.
Collaborative Research Opportunity:
The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases is seeking statements of capability or interest from parties interested in collaborative research to further develop, evaluate, or commercialize this technology. For collaboration opportunities, please contact Jonathan Motley at 240-669-5209, or
jonathan.motley@nih.gov.

AGENCY:
Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Establishment of Federal Advisory committee.
SUMMARY:
The DoD (referred to herein as “the Department of War” or “DoW”) is publishing this notice to announce it is establishing the Advisory Council on Health and Human Performance Optimization (“the Council”) as a discretionary Federal advisory committee.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jim Freeman, Advisory Committee Management Officer for the DoW, 703-692-5952.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In August 2026 and in accordance with authority described in Chapter 10 of Title 5 United States Code (U.S.C.) 1008(a)(2), the Secretary of War (SecWar) approved the establishment of the Council. The public or interested organizations may submit written statements about the Council's mission and functions.
The Council will operate in accordance with chapter 10 of title 5, U.S.C. (“commonly known as the Federal Advisory Committee Act” or “FACA”), and 41 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 102-3, “Federal Advisory Committee Management,” [90
Federal Register
58417; December 16, 2025], and DoW policies and procedures.
Written statements may be submitted at any time or in response to the stated agenda of planned meetings of the Council. All written statements shall be submitted to the Council Designated Federal Officer (DFO), CAPT Shawn Clausen, U.S. Navy, 703-275-6060, or
shawn.s.clausen.mil@health.mil.
The DFO will ensure all written statements are provided to the membership for their consideration. Consistent with 41 CFR 102-3.65(a), the DoW is publishing the Council's Public Interest Determination.
Pursuant to 41 CFR 102-3.60(a), to establish, renew, reestablish, or merge a discretionary (agency discretion) advisory committee, an agency must first consult with the General Services Administration's Committee Management Secretariat (the Secretariat) and, as part of the consultation, provide a written public interest determination approved by the head of the agency to the Secretariat with a copy to the Office of Management and Budget. In addition, pursuant to 41 CFR 102-3.35, an agency shall follow the same consultation process and document in writing the same determination of need before creating a subcommittee under a discretionary committee that is not made up entirely of members of a parent advisory committee.
Information on the following factors for the Council is provided to the Secretariat to demonstrate that establishing the Council is in the public interest:
1.
Annual Budget:
The DoW estimates annual operating costs to support the Council are $1,368,170, which includes personnel travel, meetings, and contract support.
a.
Federal personnel on a full-time equivalent basis:
The estimated annual personnel costs to the DoW are 1.5 full-time equivalent at $422,043, which includes basic pay with cost-of-living allowance.
b.
Other Federal internal costs:
$861,127.
c.
Proposed payments to members:
Consistent with 10 U.S.C. 173, members of the Council are not compensated for their services, except for travel and per diem reimbursement for official Council-related business.
d.
Proposed number of members:
As authorized by the SecWar, the Council will be composed of not more than 20 members and subcommittees, if authorized, will be composed of not more than 15 members.
e.
Reimbursable costs:
The estimated reimbursement costs, to include travel, for Advisory Committee on Health and Human Performance Optimization staff and members are $85,000.
2.
If applicable, the total dollar value of grants expected to be recommended during the fiscal year:
N/A.
3.
Criteria for selecting members to ensure the committee has the necessary expertise and balanced membership:
As described in its proposed charter and membership balance plan, Council members will be talented, innovative private and public sector health care leaders and membership shall be drawn from individuals with expertise in any of the following disciplines:
(a) Urology/Andrology
(b) Endocrinology
(c) Nutrition
(d) Neurology/Brain Health
(e) Combat Stress Physiology/Military Operational Medicine
(i) Orthopedics/Sports Medicine/Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
(j) Digital Health and Wearable Technology
(k) Psychiatry/Psychology/Spiritual Resilience
(l) Sleep Medicine
(m) Strategic Foresight and Biomedical Innovation/Human Factors Engineering
In evaluating candidates for the Council, the DoW considers education, life experience, and professional credentials concerning the subject matters anticipated to be tasked to the Council. The DoW has found that viewing the complex issues facing the DoW through a multidisciplinary advisory committee provides the DoW and, more importantly, the American public with a broader understanding of the issues on which subsequent policy decisions are based. Membership shall be fairly balanced in terms of points of view represented and the functions to be performed by the Council. The Council's membership balance is not static, and the DoW Appointing Authority may change the membership based upon work assigned to the Council.
5.
Justification that the information or advice provided by the Federal advisory committee or subcommittee is not available from another Federal advisory committee, another Federal Government source, or any other more cost-effective and less burdensome source:
The Council will serve as a high-impact, low-cost mechanism for the DoW to secure the expertise of the nation's foremost leaders at the nexus of warrior health and performance. The Council will provide knowledge derived from extensive experience with issues, techniques, and strategies that impact, optimize, and re-establish well-being and performance in the face of challenging circumstances. This expertise is essential to accelerate evaluation and potential applications of strategies to improve human performance among members of the DoW Active and Reserve Components, to maintain a ready fighting force on the leading edge of lethality, and to better care for those suffering from operational stressors and exposures.

articles.title: Determination That PEPCID RPD (Famotidine) Orally Disintegrating Tablets, 20 Milligrams and 40 Milligrams Were Not Withdrawn From Sale for Reasons of Safety or Effectiveness
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA, Agency, or we) has determined that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 milligrams (mg) and 40 mg, were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. This determination will allow FDA to approve abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) for famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, if all other legal and regulatory requirements are met.
articles.full_text:
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 355(j)) allows the submission of an ANDA to market a generic version of a previously approved drug product. To obtain approval, the ANDA applicant must show, among other things, that the generic drug product: (1) has the same active ingredient(s), dosage form, route of administration, strength, conditions of use, and (with certain exceptions) labeling as the listed drug, which is a version of the drug that was previously approved, and (2) is bioequivalent to the listed drug. ANDA applicants do not have to repeat the extensive clinical testing otherwise necessary to gain approval of a new drug application (NDA).
Section 505(j)(7) of the FD&C Act requires FDA to publish a list of all approved drugs. FDA publishes this list as part of the “Approved Drug Products With Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations,” which is known generally as the “Orange Book.” Under FDA regulations, drugs are removed from the list if the Agency withdraws or suspends approval of the drug's NDA or ANDA for reasons of safety or effectiveness or if FDA determines that the listed drug was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness (21 CFR 314.162).
A person may petition the Agency to determine, or the Agency may determine on its own initiative, whether a listed drug was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. This determination may be made at any time after the drug has been withdrawn from sale, but must be made prior to approving an ANDA that refers to the listed drug (§ 314.161 (21 CFR 314.161)). FDA may not approve an ANDA that does not refer to a listed drug.
                    PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, are the subject of NDA 020752, held by Merck & Co., Inc., and initially approved on May 29, 1998. PEPCID RPD is indicated for short term treatment of active duodenal ulcer, maintenance therapy for duodenal ulcer patients at reduced dosage after healing of an active ulcer, short term treatment of active benign gastric ulcer, short term treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease, and treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions (
                    e.g.,
                     Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome, multiple endocrine adenomas).
                
                    In a letter dated September 11, 2013, Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp., (Merck) notified FDA that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were being discontinued, and FDA moved the drug product to the “Discontinued Drug Product List” section of the Orange Book. In the same letter, Merck Sharp requested withdrawal of NDA 020752 for PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg. In the 
                    Federal Register
                     of June 21, 2017 (82 FR 28322), FDA announced that it was withdrawing approval of NDA 020752, effective July 21, 2017.
                
Lachman Consultant Services, Inc. submitted a citizen petition dated June 29, 2026 (Docket No. FDA-2026-P-7178), under 21 CFR 10.30, requesting that the Agency determine whether PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
After considering the citizen petition and reviewing Agency records and based on the information we have at this time, FDA has determined under § 314.161 that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. The petitioner has identified no data or other information suggesting that these drug products were withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. We have carefully reviewed our files for records concerning the withdrawal of PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, from sale. We have also independently evaluated relevant literature and data for possible postmarketing adverse events. We have reviewed the available evidence and determined that this drug product was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
Accordingly, the Agency will continue to list PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, in the “Discontinued Drug Product List” section of the Orange Book. The “Discontinued Drug Product List” delineates, among other items, drug products that have been discontinued from marketing for reasons other than safety or effectiveness. ANDAs that refer to these drug products may be approved by the Agency as long as they meet all other legal and regulatory requirements for the approval of ANDAs. If FDA determines that labeling for these drug products should be revised to meet current standards, the Agency will advise ANDA applicants to submit such labeling.
                    Grace R. Graham,
Deputy Commissioner for Policy, Legislation, and International Affairs.

AGENCY:
Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Treasury.
                    ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comments.
                    SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the IRS is inviting comments on the information collection request outlined in this notice.
                    DATES:
Written comments should be received on or before December 28, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        Direct all written comments to Andres Garcia, Internal Revenue Service, Room 6526, 1111 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20224, or by email to 
                        pra.comments@irs.gov. Include “OMB Control No. 1545-1628” in the subject line of the message.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IRS, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)), provides the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps the IRS assess the impact and minimize the burden of its information collection requirements. Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record, and viewable on relevant websites. For this reason, please do not include in your comments information of a confidential nature, such as sensitive personal information. Comments are invited on: (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and (e) estimates of capital or start-up costs and costs of operation, maintenance, and purchase of services to provide information.

                     Communications Excise Tax; Prepaid Telephone Cards.

The regulations provide rules for the application of the communications excise tax to prepaid telephone cards.

                     Extension of a currently approved collection.
                
                    Affected Public:
                     Business or other for-profit.

                     34.

Tax Analyst.

AGENCY:
Office of the General Counsel, HUD.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Section 106 of the Department of Housing and Urban Development Reform Act of 1989 (the HUD Reform Act) requires HUD to publish quarterly
Federal Register
notices of all regulatory waivers that HUD has approved. Each notice covers the quarterly period since the previous
Federal Register
notice. The purpose of this notice is to comply with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act. This notice contains a list of regulatory waivers granted by HUD during the period beginning on January 1, 2026 and ending on March 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For general information about this notice, contact Amanda Wahlig, Acting Associate General Counsel for Legislation and Regulations, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Room 10282, Washington, DC 20410-0500, telephone 202-708-3055 (this is not a toll-free number). HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit:
https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/telecommunications-relay-service-trs.
For information concerning a particular waiver that was granted and for which public notice is provided in this document, contact the person whose name and address follow the description of the waiver granted in the accompanying list of waivers that have been granted in the first quarter of calendar year 2026.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act added a new section 7(q) to the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act (42 U.S.C. 3535(q)), which provides that:
1. Any waiver of a regulation must be in writing and must specify the grounds for approving the waiver;
2. Authority to approve a waiver of a regulation may be delegated by the Secretary only to an individual of Assistant Secretary or equivalent rank, and the person to whom authority to waive is delegated must also have authority to issue the particular regulation to be waived;
3. Not less than quarterly, the Secretary must notify the public of all waivers of regulations that HUD has approved, by publishing a notice in the
Federal Register
. These notices (each covering the period since the most recent previous notification) shall:
a. Identify the project, activity, or undertaking involved;
b. Describe the nature of the provision waived and the designation of the provision;
c. Indicate the name and title of the person who granted the waiver request;
d. Describe briefly the grounds for approval of the request; and
e. State how additional information about a particular waiver may be obtained.
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act also contains requirements applicable to waivers of HUD handbook provisions that are not relevant to the purpose of this notice.
This notice follows procedures provided in HUD's Statement of Policy on Waiver of Regulations and Directives issued on April 22, 1991 (56 FR 16337). In accordance with those procedures and with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act, waivers of regulations are granted by the Assistant Secretary with jurisdiction over the regulations for which a waiver was requested. In those cases in which a General Deputy Assistant Secretary granted the waiver, the General Deputy Assistant Secretary was serving in the absence of the Assistant Secretary in accordance with the office's Order of Succession.
This notice covers waivers of regulations granted by HUD from January 1, 2026 through March 31, 2026. For ease of reference, the waivers granted by HUD are listed by HUD program office (for example, the Office of Community Planning and Development, the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, the Office of Housing, and the Office of Public and Indian Housing, etc.). Within each program office grouping, the waivers are listed sequentially by the regulatory section of title 24 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) that is being waived. For example, a waiver of a provision in 24 CFR part 58 would be listed before a waiver of a provision in 24 CFR part 570.
Where more than one regulatory provision is involved in the grant of a particular waiver request, the action is listed under the section number of the first regulatory requirement that appears in 24 CFR and that is being waived. For example, a waiver of both § 58.73 and § 58.74 would appear sequentially in the listing under § 58.73.
Waiver of regulations that involve the same initial regulatory citation are in time sequence beginning with the earliest-dated regulatory waiver.
Should HUD receive additional information about waivers granted during the period covered by this report (the first quarter of calendar year 2026) before the next report is published (the second quarter of calendar year 2026), HUD will include any additional waivers granted for the first quarter in the next report.
( printed page 67599)
Accordingly, information about approved waiver requests pertaining to HUD regulations is provided in the Appendix that follows this notice.
David Woll,
General Counsel.

AGENCY:
U.S. International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that on October 20, 2026, the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”) issued an Initial Determination on Violation of Section 337 and Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bond. The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. This notice is soliciting comments from the public and interested government agencies only.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joelle Justus, Esq., Office of the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-2593. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov.
For help accessing EDIS, please email
EDIS3Help@usitc.gov.
General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server at
https://www.usitc.gov.
Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 provides that, if the Commission finds a violation, it shall exclude the articles concerned from the United States unless, after considering the effect of such exclusion upon the public health and welfare, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, and United States consumers, it finds that such articles should not be excluded from entry. (19 U.S.C. 1337(d)(1)). A similar provision applies to cease and desist orders. (19 U.S.C. 1337(f)(1)).
The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. The recommended relief includes a limited exclusion order directed to vaporizer devices, cartridges used therewith, and components thereof imported, sold for importation, and/or sold after importation by respondents Glas, Inc. and Glas, LLC that infringe claims 1, 5, 7, 15-16, and 18-21 of U.S. Patent No. 11,134,722 and claims 1, 5, and 8 of U.S. Patent No. 11,606,981. The recommended relief also includes a cease and desist order directed to the Glas respondents. Parties are to file public interest submissions pursuant to 19 CFR 210.50(a)(4).
The Commission is interested in further development of the record on the public interest in this investigation. Accordingly, members of the public and interested government agencies are invited to file submissions of no more than five (5) pages, inclusive of attachments, concerning the public interest in light of the ALJ's Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bonding issued in this investigation on October 20, 2026. Comments should address whether issuance of the recommended remedial orders in this investigation, should the Commission find a violation, would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) Explain how the articles potentially subject to the recommended remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) Identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the recommended orders;
(iii) Identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) Indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third-party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the recommended orders within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) Explain how the recommended orders would impact consumers in the United States.
Written submissions must be filed no later than by close of business on November 19, 2026.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above pursuant to 19 CFR 210.4(f). Submissions should refer to the investigation number (“Inv. No. 337-TA-1464”) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (

AGENCY:
U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Call for nominations.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is soliciting nominations for the position of an Interventional Radiologist on the Advisory Committee on the Medical Uses of Isotopes (ACMUI). Nominees should currently be practicing as an Interventional Radiologist.
DATES:
Nominations are due on or before December 28, 2026.
Nomination Process:
Submit an electronic copy of resume or curriculum vitae, along with a cover letter, to Ms. Sarah Hoenig,
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov.
The cover letter should describe the nominee's current duties and responsibilities and express the nominee's interest in the position. Please ensure that the resume or curriculum vitae includes the following information, if applicable: education; certification(s); professional association and committee membership activities; duties and responsibilities in current and previous clinical, research, and/or academic position(s).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Sarah Hoenig, U.S Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards; 301-415-3284;
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
ACMUI members possess the medical and technical skills needed to address evolving issues. The current membership is comprised of the following professionals: (a) nuclear medicine physician; (b) nuclear cardiologist; (c) two radiation oncologists; (d) diagnostic radiologist; (e) therapy medical physicist; (f) nuclear medicine physicist; (g) nuclear pharmacist; (h) radiation safety officer; (i) patients' rights advocate; (j) Food and Drug Administration representative; (k) Agreement State representative; and (l) interventional radiologist (vacant). For additional information about membership on the ACMUI, visit the ACMUI Membership web page,
http://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/regulatory/advisory/acmui/membership.html.
The ACMUI Interventional Radiologist provides advice on issues associated with the regulation of interventional radiology applications of byproduct material. This advice includes providing input on NRC proposed rules and guidance, providing recommendations on the training and experience requirements for Authorized Interventional Radiologists, identifying medical events associated with these uses, evaluating non-routine uses of byproduct material, bringing key issues in the interventional radiology community to the attention of NRC staff, radiation safety and NRC medical-use policy. This individual is appointed based on his or her educational background, certification(s), work experience, involvement and/or leadership in professional society activities, and other information obtained in letters or during the selection process.
Nominees must be U.S. citizens and be able to devote approximately 160 hours per year to ACMUI business. Members are expected to attend semi-annual full-day virtual meetings and to participate in other shorter teleconferences or virtual meetings, as needed. ACMUI members who present during the annual ACMUI Commission Briefing Meeting, may need to travel to attend these meetings in-person at NRC HQs in Rockville, MD. Committee members currently serve a four-year term and may be considered for reappointment to an additional term.
( printed page 67624)
Members who are not Federal employees at the time of their appointment are compensated for their service. In addition, members are reimbursed for travel (including per diem in lieu of subsistence) and are reimbursed secretarial and correspondence expenses. Full-time Federal employees are reimbursed for travel expenses only.
Security Background Check:
The selected nominee will undergo a thorough security background check. Security paperwork may take the nominee several weeks to complete.
Nominees will also be required to complete a financial disclosure statement to avoid conflicts of interest.
Dated at Rockville, Maryland, this 23 of October, 2026.
